Hon. MURRAY MacLAREN (Minister of Pensions and National Health) moved that the house go into committee at the next sitting to consider the following proposed resolution :
That it is expedient to amend the Pension Act to give effect to certain recommendations of the committee appointed to investigate the administration of the act; to provide for the elimination of various provisions relating to the pension tribunal; and for an increase in the number of members of the commission and to prescribe their tenure of office; for the continuation of the pension appeal court as a court of appeal and of review; for the appointment of an ad hoc judge as a member of the pension appeal court and his remuneration; for the appointment of a travelling inspector of the veterans' bureau, and of pension counsel, and a reviewing officer; for the payment of awards by the comptroller of the treasury, and generally to simplify and improve procedure under the act.

General, having been made acquainted with the subject matter of this resolution, recommends it to the favourable consideration of the house.

On the orders of the day:

I
have a question to ask the Minister of Labour. It is based on a report appearing in a newspaper published in my riding. The Canadian Legion made an appeal to Victoria, the capital of the province, for further assistance for the unemployed and to take care of those being evicted. The answer came back from Victoria, from the Minister of Finance, to the effect that in his opinion the allowances *were inadequate but that they were doing the best they could, and that, in the meantime, the federal government was in arrears to the province to the extent of $2,000,000. Is that report correct?

speakeroldname: Hon. W. A. GORDON (Minister of Labour):
speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: The question only illustrates again the undesirability of relying upon newspaper reports. The hon. member was good enough to intimate to me that he would ask the question. The Dominion government does not owe the province of British Columbia $2,000,009; $185,910.42 is the total of the accounts at present in the Labour department, $100,000 of that amount of accounts being received only to-day. It takes about five days to a week to have the accounts passed through the various departments of government for payment. I can assure the hon. member that the report in the newspaper is not correct.
My private opinion is-
Order.

The house resumed from Wednesday, April 12, consideration in committee of Bill No. 37, respecting the Canadian National Railways and to provide for cooperation with the Canadian Pacific Railway system and for other purposes-Mr. Manion.-Mr. Gobeil in the chair.
On section 3 (h)-Tribunal.

An amendment had been moved by the hon. member for Swift Current (Mr. Bothweli) to subsection (h) of section 3. As I recall it, the discussion was in connection with a point raised by the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston) as to whether the Canadian National system could abandon lines without the consent of the Board of Railway Commissioners and the governor in council. The opinion of the hon. member was that inasmuch as the Canadian National company had taken over the operations and management of the entire structure, no portion could be abandoned without the consent of the Board of Railway Commissioners and the authority of the governor in council. The committee was discussing this point when it rose at six o'clock on Wednesday and I was wondering whether the minister had looked into the matter and was prepared to make a statement.

It is the desire of the government that this bill should be as acceptable as possible to all sections of the house, and to that end, I intend to make a suggestion. Before making this suggestion, may I say that the Duff commission were very strongly of the opinion that as far as possible wre should endeavour to have the National railways so managed as not to be subject to pressure of any kind either from members of the house or members of any government. In other words, it was felt that in so far as it
C.N.R.-C.P.B. Bill

was possible we should endeavour to place the Canadian National Railways in such a position that they could be managed as a private railway company would be managed and not subject to what might be termed political or public pressure. For these reasons, it is the desire of the government that so far as possible we should avoid referring to the governor in council matters which have been decided upon by the trustees. The moment you get back to the governor in council, you get back to political pressure of some kind from the party in power, or the other.
Only the one party, not the other.

In order to comply with the suggestion of the Duff commission and at the same time not leave the management open to political pressure, it has been suggested that an amendment should be made to section 2. This amendment will provide that lines may not be abandoned without the approval of the Board of Railway Commissioners, and I think it will appeal to hon. members opposite as being a reasonable and satisfactory solution of the difficulty. We have no desire that the trustees should be in a position to do anything but good for the Canadian National Railways. At the same time we have no desire to get away from the recommendation of the commission that the railways should be kept free from political or public pressure. Section 2 has been allowed to stand but this amendment can be proposed when the committee is again considering that section. It will be remembered that section 2 is a preliminary section and applies to the bill as a whole. For that reason it will probably be better to have the amendment made to that particular section. The suggested amendment reads:
Notwithstanding anything in this act or any other act, no railway company-
This would apply to the Canadian Pacific as well as to the Canadian National Railways. -shall abandon the operation of any line of railway or any part thereof without obtaining the approval of the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada of such abandonment.

Would
that apply to the operation of the railway docks located at Vancouver?

No. We have tried to word this amendment so that it would not apply to those railway activities which it is felt should be operated more in a cooperative spirit than they have been in the past. There is no reason why running rights over certain lines should be interfered with, and there is no 
reason why the docks at Vancouver, for instance, should not be operated jointly. The fear has been expressed by 'hon. members, possibly with some ground, that the board of trustees, either acting for themselves, for the Canadian National Railways or in an endeavour to cooperate with the Canadian Pacific, either with or without an arbitral board, could abandon portions of the Canadian National. I think that is the conclusion which might be drawn from the discussion which has taken place, and it was thought that if the Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific had to obtain the approval of the Board of Railway Commissioners before any abandonment could take place, it would be reasonably satisfactory to all portions of the house.

Would the decision of
the Board of Railway Commissioners be final?

Yes. I would refer the
committee to clause (e) of section 17 of part III of the bill. It must be remembered that this part of the bill deals with the arbitral tribunals. Subsection (3) of section 17 states that the powers of the tribunals shall extend to the abandonment of lines, services or facilities and in view of the amendment which has been suggested, it will be necessary to eliminate at least- that part of clause (e) of this section which deals with abandonment of lines. The committee could decide later on whether it desires to eliminate that part of the clause dealing with services or facilities. It would thus be made clear that in so far as the abandonment of lines was concerned, the Board of Railway Commissioners would be supreme over an arbitral tribunal.

As a matter of information
I should like to ask the minister what is the position under the present act. Is it possible for the board to abandon lines?
' Mr. MANION:	That was the question
we were discussing very fully the other day.

There is mo certainty about
it?

I think there is, according to my information. The Canadian Pacific could abandon any part of its system except the main line, and the Canadian National, iwith the exception of the Grand Trunk, could abandon portions of its lines without submission to the Board of Railway Commissioners, and in some cases without submission to the govenor in council. As I said before, the Canadian Pacific can abandon any portion of their system, with the exception of the (main line. This amendment would put a restriction upon the Canadian Pacific as well as

upon the Canadian National. I may say quite frankly that I have not discussed this amendment with the Canadian Pacific to see whether or not they would be pleased with it; I do not know their attitude.

I am sure they would be
delighted.

I am not so sure; I
should not be surprised if the Canadian Pacific did not care to have an amendment of this kind, but we have not had time to submit it to either railway company. I am submitting it now to the committee as a reasonable compromise arrangement which I think should be fairly satisfactory to all parties in the house.

Under this proposed
amendment would the public be in the same position in regard to the abandonment of lines as they are to-day, with respect to the Board of Railway Commissi oners?

As a matter of fact I
think they would be in a far better position. As I pointed out before, the Canadian Pacific could abandon some of ite lines without submission, and 'the Canadian National, according to the advice of those learned in legal lore, could abandon limes, with the exception of those of the Grand Trunk, without submission to the board. By this amendment neither company could abandon a line without submission ito 'the board, so I think the public is protected to a greater extent.

Do I understand that under
the amendment suggested by the minister no railway line shall be abandoned unless that is agreed to by the Board of Railway Commissioners? How would that affect lines which are partially constructed? Would the same thing apply; before such lines were abandoned would the matter have to be submitted to the railway commission?

May I
remind the committee that the proposed amendment reads:
-shall abandon the operation of any line

I was going to point out
that this W'ould apply only to the abandonment of lines that were in operation, but the chairman has just pointed out that fact. I know the line to which my bom. friend is referring, the Sunny Brae-Guysborough branoh, which is in his riding, and in that of my hon. friend from Piotou. There is no reason why this amendment would place that proposed line, which is partially constructed, in any different position than it is in to-day, because it is not in operation and therefore would not be affected by the amendment. The
question of the completion of that line would remain in the hands of the Canadian National Railway Company, as it is to-day; it will be completed when they think it wise to do so.
Would this legislation, if adopted, override existing contracts with muneipalities which subsidized the construction and operation of branch lines?
No.
I understood the minister to say that he was not going to move this amendment just now.
The only reason I did not move it was that we happened to be dealing with section 3, but if the committee wishes to do so we can go back to section 2, and I will be glad to move it.
I would prefer not to have that done, because I should like to consider the amendment first.

I laid it on the table because I thought it might save a good deal of discussion; several times my hon. friend from Quebec South proposed that we should lay our amendments on the table in order to give hon. gentlemen time to consider them. While I am on the subject of amendments there is another point with which I might deal. There has been a good deal of discussion with regard to the possibility of amalgamation, and my right hon. leader and I have both told the house and the committee that it is not the intention of the government to permit amalgamation. We have both stated that an amendment would be moved designed to prevent any amalgamation, and perhaps since I am laying one amendment on the table so that hon. members may have an opportunity to study it, with the hope of curtailing unnecessary discussion and perhaps shortening the time we must spend on this bill, I might read to the house the amendment dealing with amalgamation, a copy of which I shall send across to hon. gentlemen opposite. Probably this amendment will be moved as the last clause of the bill, so that it will apply to the whole act. The proposed amendment is as follows:
Nothing in this act shall be deemed to authorize the amalgamation of any railway company which is comprised in national railways with any railway company which is comprised in Pacific railways, nor to authorize the unified management and control of the railway system which forms part of national railways and the railway system which forms part of Pacific railways.
That sounds a little complicated, but in view of the many acts which have been passed by this house at various times with regard to the organization of the Canadian National rail-
C.N.R.-C.P.R. Bill

way system it is necessary to put this amendment in this form. To show how difficult it is to get an amendment fully covering the intention of the government may I say that this morning there was a good deal of difference of opinion among those of us who were considering the matter, with regard to two different amendments, the one I have read and another, both drawn with the intention of preventing amalgamation. Finally, after the matter was submitted to the Department of Justice and considered there, with the object of getting an amendment which would prevent anything in the way of amalgamation of the two companies in any manner whatever, this amendment was approved by the Department of Justice.

I should like
to direct my 'hon. friend's attention to some ivords appearing in one section of the bill which I suggest might very properly be added to the proposed amendment. I would suggest that at the end of the amendment my hon. friend might add the words found in subsection 4 of section 9, preceding them by a reference to the section so that it would read as follows:
The provisions of this act, in so far .us they may be inconsistent with the provisions of this section, shall be read in the light hereof and be construed so as to conform herewith.
If that additional clause was incorporated in the amendment proposed by the minister, it would make the meaning wholly clear.

I will take that suggestion into consideration; of course I cannot decide upon it at the moment. I do not think the words would make the amendment any stronger, because it says very distinctly that nothing in this act shall be deemed to authorize amalgamation, so I think the point is amply covered. But I will give consideration to the suggestion of my right hon. friend and discuss it with my legal advisers a little later. I do not know that I could pass an opinion upon it at the moment.

I should like to ask the minister whether it will be necessary still for the governor in council to approve certain abandonments. As I understood the argument of the Prime Minister a week ago last Friday night it was that section 23 of the Canadian National Railways Act is still in force and that the trustees merely have the powers of the directors with regard to the abandonment of portions of the Canadian National railway system. If the Prime Minister was correct in that contention it would appear to me that even if we pass this amendment the position will be that with regard to parts of the Cana-

dian National system it will be necessary to have the approval not only of the Board of Railway Commissioners but also of the governor in council. Is that the understanding of the administration?

The whole question is so
complicated and involved at times that I do not like to answer too definitely. If I may speak subject to possible correction a little later, though I think I am right, I would say that in regard to the government railways such as the Intercolonial, for example-since the Intercolonial has been entrusted to the Canadian National for operation, by order in council-I do believe that before any part could be abandoned, in addition to the approval of the Board of Railway Commissioners, which is covered by this proposed amendment, the approval of the governor in council would be necessary also.

Under section 23 of the
Canadian National Railways Act?

Perhaps. This is a very
complicated matter and I do not know that I wish to say specifically that it would be under that section. As I pointed out the other evening, so far as my information goes section 23 applies specifically to the Grand Trunk, which was the only road to be amalgamated with the Canadian National Railway Company. I do believe as well that with regard to the government railways, such as the Intercolonial, the National Transcontinental and the Prince Edward Island railway, in addition to the approval of the Board of Railway Commissioners there would have to be further approval by order in council. They have been entrusted to the Canadian National for operation; that was done by order in council, and therefore I think any abandonment would require to be approved by order in council as well.
In the event of the Hudson Bay railway being incorporated with the Canadian National for administrative purposes, it would apply to that also?

The Hudson Bay railway
has never been incorporated with the Canadian National. It is merely operated bs' the Canadian National as agents for the government.
I prefaced my question with the words "in the event of." In the event of the Hudson Bay railway being incorporated with the Canadian National, it would be in the same position?

Yes.

C.N.R.-C.P.R. Bill

Do I understand that an
amendment is to be proposed to take away from the tribunal the power to order the abandonment of lines?
That is right.

I do not know whether I am in order now, but I should like to put a question to the minister for information. It affects the whole act and I have never heard any explanation in regard to it. In what way does this bill affect the lines of the Canadian National Railways in the United States?

The lines in the United
States are not affected at all so far as cooperation with the Canadian Pacific is concerned. That is as regards Part II. Nor are they affected so far as Part III of the bill is concerned which deals with the arbitral tribunal. But so far as Part I is concerned, the American lines are affected just the same as any other portion of the Canadian National Railways, because Part I applies to the Canadian National Railway Company alone; it does not apply in any way to the Canadian Pacific as regards cooperation or otherwise. My legal adviser points out that the trustees are not the directors, and that is true. When the new trustees are appointed they will not be the directors of either the Grand Trunk Western or the Central Vermont, because by the laws of the United States these lines have to have certain groups of directors. They are both American corporations and naturally they have to be managed according to the regulations of the Interstate Commerce Commission, so in that respect they are in a somewhat different position. So far as Part I can apply to those roads it would apply; but so rar as cooperation with the Canadian Pacihc ;s concerned, that does not apply at all in regard to Part I of the bill.
For further information, is not the board of directors of the Canadian National railway system also the board of directors of the lines owned by the Canadian National in the United States?
No. They have their own separate boards of directors, both the Central Vermont and the Grand Trunk Western.

I take it from the
minister's reply that when this bill becomes law the trustees will have no jurisdiction over the lines in the United States?

That is quite true so far
as aobuial management is concerned, but of *course they will have supervision over those lines in a general way just as the board of
directors to-day has general supervision over them as a part of the Canadian National railway. I do not know if I have made the difference clear to my hon. friend.

Perhaps it is my fault that I do not quite see the difference. What I should like to know is this: If this bill becomes law, who will control the lines of the Canadian National in the United States? Who will have the management of them?

The trustees will have the management so far as the board of directors now have the management. They will be general snpervisors, if I may put it in that way, of the whole Canadian National railway system. In addition, there is a board of directors of the Grand Trunk Western and of the Central Vermont, some of whom are directors as well of the Canadian National in Canada, and some of whom are Americans. Through these boards these American lines would be managed subject to the control of the trustees as to financing, and generally in an advisory way.

Will the new board of
trustees have representation on these American boards?
Yes, no doubt.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: We own all the shares.

Will one of the trustees be
on each board?

For example, some of the
directors of the Canadian National are also directors of the Grand Trunk Western. My deputy minister is a director of both of them, and so is Mr. Hungerford; Mr. Grant, the financial comptroller, is also one of the directors over there. That might have to be changed, but perhaps not. It is quite probable that one of the trustees, or possibly two, would be directors on the boards of the United States, but I have not thought that out sufficiently.

When this bill was first before the committee the Minister of Railways promised to get certain information in regard to the effect of cooperation or the consolidation of train services between Montreal and Toronto and Ottawa and Toronto. I would ask him if he has that information now and if he will give it to the committee.

I am sorry I have not
that information. I must confess that I have overlooked that detail. I remember quite well that my bon. friend wanted information
C.N.R.-C.P.R. Bill

as to what would be the effects on labour of the general cooperative scheme. I looked into that matter and found that that information was not available. I am afraid that I have neglected to secure the information my horn, friend now asks for as to the decrease in labour employment because of the pooling of trains between Montreal and Toronto and Ottawa and Toronto, but I shall be glad to get it for him.

There was more than that involved. There was also the question of the anticipated financial saving as a result of this consolidation of services. I should like to go even further than that. The dividing line between consolidation of services and cooperation or amalgamation is so thin that any subsequent enactment against amalgamation does not mean anything 'because by this bill to all intents and purposes we are going to have cooperation or the amalgamation of services under two managements instead of one. In the case of the consolidation of services between Montreal and Toronto, and Ottawa and Toronto, for instance, to all intents and purposes there you have amalgamation under Canadian Pacific and Canadian National management, and what I should like to know is what are the anticipated savings over a certain period of timie for the Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific as a result of that consolidation of services. Secondly, what is the amount of labour that has been displaced as a result of that same consolidation of services. While the minister is obtaining that information I think he might go a little further. As I said on a previous occasion, it is common knowledge that efforts are already being made by the two railways to bring about greater consolidation and cooperation of services right across the country. In the last few days I have been among a great many railway men, and the spirit of these men has been completely broken down by the bill that is now before the house. Men with fifteen or twenty or twenty-five years of service do not know how long they are going to be kept in the employ of the railways. I know that engineers have been looking over many of the large terminals of this country on behalf of the railways to see what saving might be made by the closing down of certain terminals and the consolidation of services right across the country. I anticipate myself that in a short time, perhaps two or three years, about twenty thousand railway men will find themselves without a job. Now that is a very serious state of affairs. I do feel before the bill passes the committee hon. members ought to be fully aware of the impli-

cations involved in it. I am not so much concerned about tribunals or the powers of any board which may be appointed under the bill, but I certainly am concerned with any move to introduce legislation which will have the effect of throwing about 20,000 men out of work when, as a matter of fact there are hundreds of thousands walking the streets with no possible opportunity of being absorbed into industry. In addition to obtaining information in regard to the consolidation of services between Montreal, Ottawa and Toronto, and the effect such consolidation has had upon the financial situation of the two railways, I am asking the minister now to obtain information showing what efforts are now in progress, or what action has been taken by the two railway companies, towards cooperation in services between other terminal points in Canada.

My hon. friend asked that question a few days ago. However in listening to the discussion which followed I am afraid I overlooked the smaller detail in attempting to oblige him with information on the larger points at issue.
It is not a smaller detail.

Certainly Montreal, Ottawa and Toronto are small when compared with the whole of Canada. So far as the larger question is concerned I could not and cannot obtain information concerning it. The railway management informed me that they are only surveying the whole matter at the present time. They cannot give me any estimates and I cannot force them to give me estimates in regard to the number of men who may possibly be laid off through cooperative efforts or by pooling the use of terminals.
The hon. member has stated that about 20,000 men may be laid off. I do not in any way pretend to be an expert in railway matters, but I believe that instead of laying off men in the. near future, due to the cooperative efforts being made, the railways will be taking on men. If they do not, then I think it will be a serious matter both for the railways and the country. With all due respect may I say that some people, including some railway men themselves, to a certain extent have overlooked the present financial condition not only of the railways but of the country. The railways must effect economies or they will be in such condition that not 20,000 but more men will be laid off for some time or, at any rate, until the railways get into a better financial position than they are to-day.

C.N.R.-C.P.R. Bill
This country cannot go on paying $50,000,000 or $75,000,000 a year out of its revenues for the Canadian National Railways, without serious effect upon the whole financial structure of our country. Last year the Canadian Pacific Railway barely earned its fixed charges, or the interest on its bonds. At any rate, it has paid no dividends on its common stock, and I believe it has discontinued dividends on its preferred stock. Hon. members will see that it has barely earned sufficient to pay interest on its bonds. Therefore unless there is a revival of business, the Canadian Pacific Railway, too, will be in a very serious condition. May I add that in the last week the decrease in traffic on the Canadian National railways, and no doubt on the Canadian Pacific railway, continued. So far the traffic has continued to decrease each week in 1933, when compared with the same weeks of last year. The decrease in gross traffic has amounted to about $600,000 a week.
Could the minister give us the percentage?

Last week was about 22 per cent under the same week last year. I do not like to use percentages, because I believe thej* are dangerous in matters such as this. However the fact is that last year in gross earnings the Canadian National Railways were about $39,000,000 below the 1931 figure. So far this year the decrease has continued. There seems to be no bottom to the worldwide condition through which we are passing. Because, despite anything in the nature of criticism which may be lodged, the condition is world-wide and not confined to Canada alone. Railways in the United States are certainly in no better condition than are our Canadian lines. Many of them have gone into the hands of receivers, and unless conditions change, no doubt more will follow.
Therefore I suggest that the seriousness of the situation ought to be considered. No member of this government has any desire to see men thrown out of work. Certainly I should regret very much if this legislation should have that effect. However, coming back to my former statement, in my opinion if there is a revival in business, as there must soon be if we are to avert a complete catastrophe, the railways should be taking on men rather than laying them off, despite cooperative efforts being made.
I shall endeavour to get the information for the hon. member by to-morrow. We cannot get through this bill to-day, I am quite sure. I shall endeavour to obtain for him the
information he wishes in regard to Ottawa, Montreal and Toronto services, with the information showing the savings and the number of men involved. I may say that Mr. Hungerford and Mr. Beatty gave out a statement in connection with the pooling of the passenger services between the points in question-I believe I have a copy of it among my papers-and at the time the statement was made they counted on saving something like $500,000. They did not mention the number of men affected, but without any doubt a number will be affected temporarily, at any rate.

The minister
has spoken of the falling off in traffic on the Canadian National railways, and suggested that there might be a similar falling off on the Canadian Pacific railway. I received a communication to-day stating that quite recently arrangements had been made for sending a number of members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and their mounts from Regina to Saskatoon. The original transportation order had been placed with the Canadian National Railways, but was changed at the last moment, it is alleged, by reason of the fact that the government had directed the traffic should be given to the Canadian Pacific Railway. If that is the case, undoubtedly there must be a falling off in Canadian National Railways traffic. I should like to ask the minister whether he knows anything of this matter, also whether it is the government's policy to route government business via the national railways, or if not whether the government gives any direction concerning the routing which shall be followed?

My reply to the right
hon. gentleman is that in that connection this government acts exactly the same as did the last one. I must say that the Department of Railways and Canals gives practically all its business to the Canadian National Railways. However I made inquiries after this government came into power which disclosed to me the fact that most of the departments of government, as they did under the late government, divide their traffic about fifty-fifty between the two railways. However the Department of Railways and Canals have taken the position, which I believe was taken by the late government, that practically all our traffic, whether it be freight, express or telegraphic, should be given to the Canadian National system.
In regard to the passage of mounted police and the shipment of their mounts, and any change made concerning the routing which
C.N.R.-C.P.R. Bill

would benefit the Canadian Pacific Railway, I have no doubt there was some good reason for making the change. However I cannot make a definite statement in the matter. May I say while I am on my feet there is a great deal of misconception throughout the country in regard to a possible condition implied by the remarks by the right hon. gentleman. In certain newspapers statements are being made to the effect that it has been the object of this government to push traffic over Canadian Pacific rather than over Canadian National lines. I have made a survey of that question, because I am of the opinion that if any government-the late government, this one or any other government-endeavoured to take traffic away from the people's railway and give it to the Canadian Pacific in an unfair manner, that government would certainly be unworthy of the confidence of the Canadian people.
I certainly do not admit that this government is any different from other governments in that regard. This government, like the last government, I presume, when it was in power, has treated the Canadian National as far as traffic is concerned as fairly as possible. I do not suppose anyone would suggest, whatever government is in power, that all the traffic from that government should go to the Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific get none. There may be some who would suggest it, but it has never been done.
Why not?

My hon. friend says "Why not." Anyhow I repeat that it has never been done. After all I think the Canadian Pacific Railway should be treated fairly. The people of this country owe something to the Canadian Pacific; it is an institution of which we can well be proud, just as we can of the Canadian National once it gets back on its feet. I do not think it would be the desire of any government-even if such an unlikely thing happened as that my hon. friends should get into power-to give all the business of the government to one railway, I believe they would give some to the Canadian Pacific.
They could not do it.
The Prime Minister mentions another point, that the Canadian Pacific Railway Company is one of the largest taxpayers in this dominion.

The railways
would be all one under the existing government. There would be no Canadian Pacific.

Well, the railways might
be all one, or there might not be any railways.

If I may come
back for a moment to the question raised by my colleague from North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps); it does not seem to me that the minister has given an altogether satisfactory answer. We are not suggesting that there should not be an arrangement made for economies, but we do say that the government has some responsibility, not merely to those financially interested in the roads, but also to the employees of the roads. And as fas as we can ascertain there is nothing whatever in this legislation, nor in the amendments which are now being laid on the table by the minister, to suggest that anything is to be done in the interests of the men who are to be laid off through the various economies proposed. Now I cannot see how a railroad or a government-this is a little of both-can avoid all responsibilities of an honourable employer. The employees constitute part of this railway system, they have had a great deal to do with the building up of the system, they have been encouraged to do their best work, to stay with the company in order to help build up the system. Now it would seem that they are to be thrown aside, with only the most remote possibility of ever being taken on again. It seems to me that is not fair, it would not be fair in the case of a private employer and is especially unfair in the case of a public employer. I am not urging that these men should be continued in the poistions which they have had in the past, it may be necessary to pool certain services; but since there are to be economies effected, running perhaps to half a million or a million dollars, even in the taking off of a few trains, if these economies are to be effected, it seems to me that something should be done to help the men in the meantime. It may be that ultimately these men will be able to secure some other work, but that is an impossibility under the present circumstances. I talked to some of these men only this last week, publicly and privately. They are at their wits end to know what to do. For instance on these trains mentioned between Montreal and Toronto, I know one man who was transferred from Winnipeg, to be given an opportunity of working on that train. He has now his little house in Toronto; shortly, he expects to be on the street; no connections here in the east whatever other than his railway connection, and no possibility of being able to secure a job on the railway in the near future, much less in the general labour market outside. I do think that under these circumstances the minister should pay some attention to the suggestion that we have made that the

C.N.R.-C.P.R. Bill
immediate needs of these men-I will not say entire compensation, that is a phrase which perhaps is liable to a good many meanings- but that the immediate needs of these men who are being laid off should be a first charge on the savings to be effected. I think that is a reasonable proposal. My friend here suggests an equal charge; I do not think that, I think there ought to be a preference given the men. We are trying to provide that the bondholders shall not suffer, but even in bankruptcy proceedings the last stick cannot be taken out of a house and the family left helpless. In most of our provinces there is a certain minimum amount exempt from seizure so that the people can manage temporarily. It seems to me we ought t-o adopt some such policy as that, make some minimum provision for these men. Now is the time to do it, when other amendments are being offered. I hope the minister will take into serious consideration the addition of a clause that will make some provision for the men displaced under the operation of the proposed legislation.

Following the remarks of the two previous speakers on this side, in 1921 a railway consolidation bill was passed in Great Britain which had for its purpose the consolidation of 120 railroads into four systems. The problem that is under discussion here this afternoon naturally confronted the British government at that time. This bill dealt only with private roads, but that government accepted the responsibility, which in my judgment is a responsibility of all governments when legislation is passed throwing on the labour market thousands of men. When my colleague from Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) was speaking I remarked that the responsibility for the men was at least equal to that to the bondholders. I believe that under these circumstances, where there is going to be a saving of possibly $75,000,000 a year, fifty per cent of that saving should be used to create a fund for the amelioration of the condition in which these unemployed railway workers will find themselves. It is true there is a section of the Railway Act, No. 179 I think, giving protection in certain cases, which will be unaffected by this legislation. But that does not begin to meet the situation. Take the towns in northern Ontario where these men have built homes, built up a community life, which towns will be wiped out by the passage of this legislation, because they are purely railroad centres. They are left in the midst of, may I say, a desolate waste, all that they
have built there will be rendered absolutely unnecessary by the passage of this bill.
I would like to read into the record-it will take some time but it may be useful-the clauses relating to the men who would have been laid off had this provision not been made in the British act. The act is chapter 55, of The Public General Acts of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, 1921:
An act to provide for the reorganization and further regulation of railways and the discharge of liabilities arising in connection with the possession of railways, and otherwise to amend the law relating to railways, and to extend the duration of the rates advisory committee.
Third Schedule
Existing Officers and Servants
The following provisions shall apply in respect to persons who at the date of the passing of this act are, and for a period of not less than five years have been, officers or servants of any constituent company or subsidiary company, and who shall not. prior to the amalgamation or absorption of such constituent or subsidiary company, have become pensioners or annuitants in accordance with the rules of any railway pension or superannuation fund of which they may be members, or have voluntarily retired, or have been removed from the service of any such constituent or subsidiary company by reason of misconduct or incapacity (all of which officers and servants are in this schedule hereinafter referred to as "existing officers and servants"):-
(1)	Every existing officer and servant shall, as from the date of amalgamation or absorption. become an officer or servant of the amalgamated company:
(2)	The amalgamated company may abolish the office or situation of any existing officer or servant which they deem unnecessary, and any existing officer or servant required to perform duties such as are not analagous or which are an unreasonable addition to those which as an officer or servant of the company from whom he was transferred he was required to perform may relinquish his office or situation:
(3)	No existing officer or servant so transferred shall, without his consent, be by reason of such transfer in any worse position in respect to the conditions of his service as a whole (including tenure of office, remuneration. gratuities, pension, superannuation, sick fund or any benefits or allowances whether obtaining legally or by customary practice of the constituent or subsidiary company) as compared with the conditions of service formerly obtaining with respect to him:
(4)	If any question arises as to whether the provisions of the last foregoing paragraph have been complied with, the question shall be referred to a standing arbitrator or board of arbitration appointed by the Lord Chancellor, and, if the arbitrator or board consider that those provisions have not been complied with, and that the officer or servant has thereby suffered loss or injury, they shall award him such sum to he paid by the amalgamated company as they think sufficient to compensate him for such loss or injury:

After the remarks of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre I looked up that act, and I -ee no reason why the government of this country should not, within the four corners of this bill, make provision for the protection of those thousands of men who will be laid off in consequence of this legislation which we are now considering. The men in the railway industry are specialists of a kind. They are men who, in my judgment, have made their contribution to the successful operation of the railways, and when they are thrown out they will have to take their place in the unskilled labour market of the country. I say, they are specialists, and they are special-

ists of a type absolutely essential to the proper conduct of a transportation industry such as we have in this country. The minister said there had been a considerable falling off in passengers even in the last week. Well, I believe that you can keep chopping off the limbs of a tree until you have no tree left. I quite agree with him that we are facing in Canada a condition that almost borders on bankruptcy in the next twelve months, but I believe that this condition has been brought about by the deliberate deflationary policy of this government. No one else is responsible for it. I think the government would be well advised to adopt the suggestions made by the small group in this corner of the house, who still have regard for the human element in our railway industry.

I do not think the small group in the corner should arrogate to itself sole regard for the human element in the railway industry. Hon. gentlemen directly opposite as well as those on this side have just as much regard for the human element as my hon. friends in the corner.
More.

Some hon. gentlemen say more, but certainly as much. The question is worthy of consideration, but I would point out to my hon. friend that it was fully argued the other day, when an amendment was moved by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and ruled out of order. I do not admit the huge figures mentioned by some speakers with regard to the numbers of men who are likely to be laid off in consequence of cooperation between the two railways. This parliament meets every few months. We shall be out of session only seven or eight months, at most ten months, before parliament meets again, and if after the passing of this legislation some amendment were found desirable, it could then be made. The passing of this bill is not the last word that will be said in this matter. It is possible that the act may require amendment. It is new legislation and, like most acts of parliament, it may require attention later on. If it is found that as a result of cooperative arrangements between the two railways amendments are necessary, they can be dealt with at the next session, although I make no promises as to what will be done-I do not wish to be misunderstood in that regard. At any rate, at the present time the government takes the position that we should pass this act and give the new trustees an opportunity to function, and the new arrangements a chance to produce results

C.N.R.-C.P.R. Bill
which we hope will tend to retain men who have been at work; and if it were found later on that something had to be done because men had been treated unjustly, because of the passing of this bill, then the matter could be brought up at the next session of parliament and dealt with at that time as the government of Canada and the House of Commons might see fit.

I am fully in agreement
with what the minister has said, but perhaps I might put my point in another way. There are a large number of people who have invested money in the railways of this country and who live in the United States and other parts of the world. These people draw dividends from the securities which they hold.
None of them are drawing a cent of dividends at the present time.
They are drawing interest.
There is quite a difference between the two.

As I understand it, a large
part of the Canadian Pacific securities are in the form of bonds.
About half.

Interest is being drawn upon
almost the total amount of the Canadian National indebtedness and these securities are held largely in the United States and Great Britain. I do not think more than fifteen per cent of the securities of the Canadian National and Canadian Pacific railways are held in Canada. These security holders draw interest amounting to millions of dollars. Why should we not follow 'the suggestion of the minister and let these people wait until next year so that we can give relief to our own Canadian people who are out of work? Let us put the boot on the other foot and see if it would not work just as well.

Last year the Canadian
Pacific Railway barely earned its bonded indebtedness. Bonds are first mortgages and how could that company say to its bondholders: We do not intend to pay you part of the interest which is due. The bondholders would at once foreclose upon the railway and put it into liquidation, just as has been done with many of the railways in the United States. It is quite true that a larger proportion of the indebtedness of the Canadian National Railways is in the form of bonds than the indebtedness of the Canadian Pacific Railway; it is true also that the Dominion of Canada has guaranteed these bonds and the only way that the payment of 53719-254
interest could be avoided would be for this country to repudiate its indebtedness. So far, Canada has not decided to take that step. Last year the Canadian Pacific barely earned enough to pay the interest upon its bonded indebtedness while the Canadian National Railways was $53,000,000 short of paying the interest upon its bonded indebtedness. My horn, friend, the other members of this committee and the taxpayers of this country are the people who are paying the interest upon this bonded indebtedness. We cannot refuse to pay that interest unless we choose to repudiate our debts. I think these facts should be kept in mind by hon. members rather than the bringing up of the bogey that employees of the railways are to be thrown out on the streets to starve in order that the bondholders may receive their interest. We are looking after the interests of the bondholders simply because we cannot help ourselves. As far as I am concerned,
I would prefer to see the indebtedness of the Canadian National Railways in the form of securities upon which dividends would not have to be paid unless earned. Unfortunately, in the wisdom or lack of wisdom of all governments, at least since 1919, it was decided that this indebtedness should be in the form of bonds. Until this country decides to repudiate its indebtedness, therefore, it cannot refuse to pay the interest upon these bonds.

The effect will be the laying
off of a vast number of men.

What about sharing the
work?

That is my interpretation of
the effects of this bill. A large number of men will be thrown out of employment as the result of the consolidation of services, as has been demonstrated by the consolidation of the services between Montreal and Toronto. The principal saving has been in the form of wages and the use of equipment. The minister says that we have to meet our obligations to these security holders, but I contend that we should choose between our own Canadian people and these security holders, the big majority of which reside outside of Canada.

How can we refuse to pay
the interest upon this bonded indebtedness without repudiating our debts? If my hon. friend will tell me how we can choose in favour of our own people and keep them in employment rather than to pay the interest to the bondholders, I should be very glad to hear any suggestion he has to offer.

C.N.R.-C.P.R. Bill
What would happen if this legislation did not go through?

The indebtedness of the
railways would probably increase.
All we are suggesting is that one of the conditions of holding down this indebtedness shall be that the men must be looked after.

If that is done we will be taking away the chance of economy. It does not matter very much whether you use money to pay men who are not required or to pay interest upon securities. It was the opinion of the Duff commission, which opinion I think is shared by all reasonable Canadian people, that these two railways must economize. It was felt that if they did not do so, the whole financial structure of the country would be endangered.

What I have to say, I say
with a good deal of hesitation because I know it will not meet with the approval of certain hon. members of this committee. I think most hon. members know that I have always been in favour of the public ownership of railways but I have always felt that a railway, even though publicly owned, could not be successful unless it were conducted as much as possible as a private business would be conducted. I have every sympathy with those who may be thrown out of employment by the measures of cooperation between the two great railways which may be possible under this bill, but if we are going to operate the national railways upon the principle to which I have just referred, we cannot follow the principles laid down by my hon. friends to my left, for whom I have every respect, and operate the^ railways mainly for the purposes of providing employment. The railways are being run by the Canadian people-I am referring to the Canadian National Railways-for the purpose of giving efficient railway service at as low a cost as possible and the employment of men to run the railways is incidental in a measure to what I have just enunciated. I agree with the minister when he states that unless something is done in the way of the elimination of waste, the railways will be in a perilous position and the whole financial structure of the country may be endangered. It becomes the duty of parliament to do whatever is possible to reduce the expenses of running the railway as a purely business proposition. There is one point to which I would direct the attention of my hon. friends; if this government is going to differentiate between classes of employees, this country will be entering upon a very big proposition. In the 
industrial and other centres many people are being thrown out of work because of the development of conditions in this country. In the city of Kitchener we have a great many furniture factories and to-day one of the largest factories is giving its employees only nine hours work per week, and only half of the usual number of employees are at present employed. This merely shows that if you are going to differentiate so far as railway employees are concerned, you will be entering upon a very difficult course. If we are going to say that because the employees of the Canadian National Railways are working for the people of Canada the government of Canada has a special duty to perform in looking after them when they are thrown out of work, I think it almost necessarily follows that we should enact legislation which will delegate to employers in other lines of industry the duty of looking after their employees when they are out of work. If we are going to adopt the principle at all it must be adopted in a general way. Then we get into an entirely new field, and what I am trying to say is this: I think in fairness to the country we cannot set the railway employees apart from other working men. If that is done with regard to the Canadian National, and the company is to carry the loss which otherwise would not be the case if some men were laid off, how can the company compete with its great rival the Canadian Pacific. I think you would have to enforce that principle also in connection with the Canadian Pacific, as you would have to enforce it in connection with other lines of industry. I hope I am not misunderstood; I have every sympathy with the employees of the railway company. I will say that if the government feels that by reason of the economies effected through the laying off of men by the national railways it is the duty of the government to look after those men, I am absolutely in accord with that position, but the burden should not be thrown upon the company as a business proposition. That is my point of view.
Something has been said as to whether the business of government departments should be given to the Canadian National Railways, and I am afraid in that regard I shall have to disagree with the minister. I believe that the Canadian National, which is owned by the Canadian people, should receive all the business the Canadian government possibly can give it. That sounds reasonable to me. Let us say a man has two businesses. He is a contractor and is putting up a building in one city, while his other business is the manufacture of construction material, such as

bricks. Would it not be absurd for that man to go to one of his competitors in order to buy the bricks necessary in the construction of the building?
Pretty far-fetched.

It is not far-fetched at all;
surely we should patronize ourselves first. If you want to put it this way, charity begins at home.

What should we do
as individuals ?

This is a free country, and
an individual can patronize any company he pleases. We ought to patronize our own line. As I said at the outset, Mr. Chairman, I know a good many hon. members will disagree with me on that point, but in the past I have always taken that position.
A good deal has been said with regard to amalgamation. I can only repeat that I do not believe this bill will do all that should be done. As many ihon. members know, I always have been in favour of complete amalgamation, and in spite of the fact that the Prime Minister repeated many times the slogan " Amalgamation never; competition ever," I think that was an unfortunate statement, and I believe in due course he will have to change it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Do	you believe in
amalgamation?

Yes; I believe in amalgamation under public ownership, not under private ownership. I think we will never get the full measure of saving and economy that is possible until we have complete amalgamation. I did not rise to make a speech on amalgamation, but that has been my position in the past, and I may as well make it clear now. I am in favour of the bill if certain amendments can be introduced, though I think it has a great many weaknesses. I am in favour of it because it goes a certain distance in the direction I should like to see it go, that is, in the saving of money in the operation of the road. Something has been said about the sharing of work. I am inclined to think that something more might be done by the railway people themselves so that the work which is available might be shared a little more equally among those who have been working for the company.
I have said perhaps a little more than I intended, Mr. Chairman, but once more I should like to make it clear that the railways must be run as a business proposition. If by reason of that it becomes necessary, unfortunately, that some men no longer may be employed, that cost should not be saddled 53719-254 J
upon the company; it should be borne by the whole country. There you enter upon a principle which is a great deal wider than simply taking care of those who lose their employment with the national system; you will have to extend it to all lines of business in Canada, and perhaps we will come to that yet.

I listened carefully to the hon. member who has just taken his seat, and I quite agree that the railways were built for service. The hon. gentleman added that they were not built to create employment, but neither were they built to create unemployment. This is an important fact. May I add that I cannot imagine any locomotive being operated by robots. Men are essential to the operation of a railway, but we must face the situation as it is and make the best of it. Many men have worked for the railway all their lives; their children have followed them, hoping that some day they might take the places of their fathers or grandfathers. While Sir Henry Thornton was president of the Canadian National he very often paid deserved tribute to his partners, the employees of the road. He understood that no railway could be run without the help, the loyalty and the devotion of the men employed by the company.
There is another point to which I should like to direct attention. In 1928 and 1929 the Canadian Pacific sold bonds to their own employees; these men were canvassed to invest their life savings in Canadian Pacific bonds. To-day, because of the decrease in traffic, those bonds do not return any interest, and as a result these employees are suffering because of their loyalty to the company. That loyalty did not impose upon them the obligation to buy railway bonds; that loyalty was shown when they did their full duty to the company. But they did more, and as a result to-day many of those men have lost their jobs and are receiving no return from their investment.
This only goes to emphasize the importance of having all the information available when discussing this question. I was very pleased to hear the hon. member for North Waterloo refer to the discrimination shown as between different classes of employees. It is most important that complete figures should be given; we should know how many engineers, firemen, conductors, trackmen, station agents, men working in shops and men working in the yards have been set back. What are the records of these men? We should have those figures for the Canadian Pacific as well as for the Canadian National. I think the Minister
C.N.R.-C.P.R. Bill

of Labour should be furnished with full information with regard to these men so that employment may be found for them elsewhere if there is no work on the railways. That is why I direct attention to the fact that nothing can be done for the railways unless we get the proper information and nothing can be done for unemployment unless we get all the facts. The government should be able to give the whole facts. We have already been given some figures which show the extent of the trouble, and we must see to it that a remedy is provided. That is why I ask for the information. I know that the Minister of Railways is well disposed. We cannot proceed to pass legislation without proper consideration. This House of Commons has been considering this bill for more than two weeks, and it would really take months of study by a group of members of the House of Commons to oome to a definite conclusion on the subject and bring down legislation which would meet all the necessities of the case. In a few days it is impossible to have this House of Commons properly consider such important legislation having such far-reaching effects on Canadian life from ocean to ocean. The legislation needs to be studied in detail. The legislation as first drafted, by whom I do not know, was so poor that the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen, leader of the government in the Senate, would not accept it. It was such poor legislation that he did not want to attach his name to it, and the legislation was changed in the Senate. It is not yet in its final shape. I sympathize fully with the Minister of Labour, but I also sympathize with all the men who have been let out of employment. I do not say that it is the fault of the minister, but I say that it is due to some of the policies of this government that the railways now have no traffic and that Canadian trade is curtailed. The railway business is only one side of Canadian life. Everything must be taken into acoount. There is trade, traffic, business. No railway can exist without such business. There must be an understanding of the whole situation, of all the factors involved. Although Lord Ashfield may be a good man, neither he nor another gentleman from the United States nor another gentleman from Toronto nor another gentleman from Montreal sitting together on a commission can decide such an important question as the railway question in this country. They can spend some time investigating the situation, and they can submit a report giving their views. But does the government say, when it gets 'the views of the commission, these are our views? The government says: Here are the views of the 
commissioners, and we accept them. The commissioners are the motive power of the government.
May I take this opportunity also to say this? When I see railway men out of jobs, I think of those who made money during the war at the expense of the people. We know of the immense profits that they have stolen from the people of this country, and instead of forcing them to pay back what they have stolen we see one of them, Joseph Flavelle, appointed a commissioner, and he is called an able business man. I think of the poor men who have nothing to eat and no work to do and who have spent their savings, and I get indignant when I think that their fate is decided by a common thief. I get indignant about that commissioner, about that war profiteer, who 'has been appointed with honest men on the transportation commission. This is a thing that no one with a head on his shoulders can understand. It must be explained to this country how the fate of these poor men, honest, hard-working, who have devoted their lives to their country in the work they were doing, should be decided upon by a man who is a millionaire, a war profiteer-lord bacon.

Mr. Chairman, before anybody else gets into the discussion, may I remind the committee that we have been on this bill now in the neighbourhood of two weeks and we have only passed two or three definitions. The whole discussion to-day, including my own remarks in reply to the hon. gentleman who brought up the subject, has without doubt been out of order. The clause now before us is paragraph (h) of clause 3, defining "Tribunal." May I suggest with all due deference that after two weeks of discussion by all sides of the house there has been a full opportunity for consideration of the principles of the bill, and the discussion which has taken place this afternoon should,
I think, have taken place on the second reading. I suggest that we try, if at all possible, to stick to the clause under consideration.
I do not wish to limit discussion in any way, but I should like to see some progress made on the bill, and I think the whole house wishes it.
The bill ought to have gone to a committee of this house; that is the whole trouble.

speechtext: That is an excuse; it is not fair.

It ought to have gone to a committee of the House of Commons. The method that has been adopted

in regard to this bill it has been suggested may be followed by my right hon. friend in connection with other bills. speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The Conservative tendencies of my right hon. friend do him credit.
I am glad to see them and his desire to cling to precedent, and I am not ungrateful to him for reminding me that I never feel bound by hoary precedent or hesitate to depart from it if by so doing I can advance the interests I have at heart. This bill is not being advanced by the discussions that have been taking place in this house. The right hon. gentleman suggests that the bill should have gone to a committee, but it is quite apparent from what has transpired during the last two weeks that a deliberate effort has been made to prevent the passage of this bill.
No.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I do not say by the right hon. gentleman. I said that a deliberate effort had been made, not by the right hon. gentleman because he has not said very much during the last two sessions, nor have the leading members of his party during the last session, but let anyone look at the debates! I may say that a perfect stranger looking at the Hansard drew my attention to it the other day and said, "The rules of your house certainly are very strange." To think that hour after hour we have been listening to what has taken place this afternoon-I have heard it five times, and I have not heard it all, except on two occasions. We have listened to a speech this afternoon which consisted of an attack against an eminent Canadian. It is not a new speech in this house, but since the war it has not been made so frequently. It does not do any credit to the Liberal party nor to the gentleman who made it, to attack in this house a man who is outside, without any opportunity to say a word in reply, and who was appointed to this commission, not from any desire to serve upon it, but at the earnest request of the people, not simply one road but both roads, who thought by reason of his great experience and great business capacity that he was best qualified to arrive at sound conclusions with respect to the question, a gentleman who rendered a service gratuitously to this country, without any desire to serve any selfish purpose. To make such an attack in this house upon such a man is certainly not encouraging to those to whom we look for public service. To be attacked in this wray in this house, and referred to in the terms used, charged with being the type of men we have heard they were, is not conducive to the accepting of public service by men who have by their great ability and talents made great business successes in this country. I mention that because I do not think that an attack of that sort is advancing the cause that we have at heart.
It is said that the trouble is that this legislation did not go to a committee of this house. The fact that it was considered by another chamber, in one of its committees, is a good reason why it should not go to another committee of this house. An ample opportunity was given in the Senate committee to consider this legislation. There may be differences of view as to whether that is sound or not, but it is clear that in the light of the speeches we have heard they have no reference to the bill itself. speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The word directors has a well defined meaning. The law usually requires that directors shall be shareholders,
and there is a provision in our statute that obviates the necessity of the directors of the Canadian National Railways holding shares. The term directors means those who direct. As this property is in the financial condition in which it is, but for the fact that the dominion has guaranteed the securities it would be in the hands of a receiver. That is the point I endeavoured to make, and I repeat it: But for the fact that this country, so long as it remains solvent, cannot permit the Canadian National Railways to go into receivership, we having guaranteed its obligations, it would be inappropriate to use the Word receiver, and therefore trustees carries the exact sense that attaches to the word, namely, those who are charged in trust with the responsibility of carrying foiward the undertakings that are mentioned in the statute itself. The word was one which it was difficult to obtain, so I was told by the commission. It is not easy to find a word with the exact shade of meaning. Receiver would carry an impression as to the insolvency of our own country.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I thank my hon. friend for reminding me of that fact. Neither the word directors nor the word receiver being quite adequate under the circumstances, the use of the word trustees sufficiently indicates the legal position of the three gentlemen to be appointed.

Is it possible for this utility-perhaps that is the proper expression-under present peculiar circumstances, ever to be in the position of receivership so long as Canada is solvent? I can only speak from the point of view of a layman, but I do not think the word that is being used convejrs the right impression. The gentlemen who are going to undertake the control and administration of the road are to be designated trustees, and personally I have very great objection to that. I do not think that any good purpose is being served by changing the name, because under no circumstances, so long as Canada is solvent, can the Canadian National Railways be declared to

be in bankruptcy; if that were the case, then the dominion itself would be bankrupt. For that reason I take very strong exception to the change. I do not think the proposed definition is applicable to the Canadian National Railways as such.

The expression trustee was first used I believe in connection with the administrators of our national system, in section 31 of the Drayton-Acworth report. Personally I have no objection to the term, but I do agree with my hon. friend from West Edmonton that it is not a happy expression. A trustee is someone who holds something in trust. We are not turning over the property to these trustees; we are simply engaging them to administer it. There is no transfer of assets to these men as is the case when a private business goes into liquidation and a receiver is appointed, or when there is a trustee for its administration. I do not think it makes a great deal of difference whether we call them trustees or not, but the Prime Minister's point is that, were the national railways a private corporation, it would be in the hands of a receiver, being administered for the shareholders; and as the road is in that unfortunate position it is necessary for the shareholders, who after all are the people of Canada, represented by every member in this House of Commons, to appoint trustees in perpetuity. I do not want to anticipate any of the sections of the bill. We have been dealing with sections that have been passed, but when we come to section 4, if I may refer to it for a moment, it will be seen that we shall have to give the governor in council power to dismiss all existing directors, and the right to appoint in the place of directors certain men who are cited as trustees. Section 4, subsection 1, would indicate that the directors of the Canadian National Railways, who have been directing, are to be succeeded by some other men who are to do something more than direct. I cannot imagine, but perhaps the Prime Minister or the Minister of Railways can explain, what these men are to do that has not been done by the directors. Certainly the financial problem is not facing them; any deficits they have are guaranteed by the government. The me problem that does seem to face them is ;he problem of the economical administration af the railways in order to reduce deficits and if possible to produce a surplus. So that in so far as the name is concerned, it matters little; what they are engaged for is the purpose of efficient management of a public utility which is owned by the people of Canada and 
which is not being handed to them in trust. They could be called commissioners. As trustees they do not own the property, nor are they asked to hold the property in trust. They are not even asked to hand the property back after they have placed it on a basis of efficient administration. A receiver is usually appointed for. one of two purposes: either to liquidate and wind up the business or to administer it more successfully than it has been, and when it is in good shape to hand it back to the shareholders. That is not the intention under this act, because these men are being appointed in perpetuity. You can call them trustees or directors, but I contend that their function is practically the same as the function of the previous directors.

I have said that the trustee must put the public interest before his own in all his dealings with the railway, and that he must have experience and good judgment. Good judgment is essential, because the trustees will be above the government and above parliament. They will be given a free hand to decide questions of vital importance to the future of this country. So the Prime Minister will have to find among his supporters or amongst those to whom he does not give the cold shoulder men with good judgment. He cannot find them among his own supporters. Will he find them in the Canadian National Railways or in the Canadian Pacific Railway? If he finds them in the Canadian Pacific, people will say that he is favouring that railway against the Canadian National, and if he finds them in the Canadian National, the country will be saddled. That is why I understand the Prime Minister's difficulty. But whether he gets the trustees from the Canadian National or the Canadian Pacific, they will have to be given a free hand provided they are men of superior intelligence, and I say superior intelligence because I believe in superior men, not in supermen. A trustee must have given proof of his ability and experience. It will not simply do for the Prime Minister to listen to advice that Joe or Tom or Sir Joe this or Sir Tom that is a fit person for trustee. He must judge the trustee by his own accomplishments, and in what field? In the field of railway business, and in that field alone. A man may be successful in other walks of life, he may be a good business man, but he is not necessarily qualified to occupy an important position having to do with the operation of railways. A sense of humour.
