Hospital Sweepstakes

After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

The house resumed from Tuesday, April 11, consideration of the motion of Mr. Power for the second reading of Bill No. 67, with respect to hospital sweepstakes, and on the proposed amendment thereto of Mr. Carmichael.

I
shall not prolong the discussion of this matter to any great length. When the hour for private and public bills expired the other night I had stated that this bill as presented introduced gambling pure and simple, and I further contended that hospitals would not be benefited by the financial assistance derived from this particular form of raising money; that is to say, they would not benefit in the long run.
May I now take a moment or two to review briefly the development of gambling, particularly towards that gambling on the smaller scale. If we follow the history of gambling in the old countries we shall recall that for a considerable time competition in horse racing involved a large amount of gambling, but that was on a different plane altogether from the sort of petty gambling which is introduced in this bill. As time went on the habit spread among a large section of the people and they began to gamble on the racing of dogs, hounds. This went on until gambling was engaged in on a still smaller scale, so that next we find people gambling on the racing of jack rabbits, then on the leaping of bullfrogs, and on a still minuter scale on the racing of cockroaches across the table or the floor, indeed, gambling on the ability of fleas to outdistance one another. In this bill we have gambling on an even more insignificant plane, because the chief virtue in the competition here is the ability of a person to draw a piece of cardboard out of a hat. There is something to be said for the person who wishes to place a bet on the ability of one horse or some other animal, to beat another in a race, but anyone who wants to be reasonable will agree I think that the ability to guess successfully the drawing a card out of a hat is not one of great significance.
This bill undertakes to legalize gambling and it undertakes to legalize the pettiest forms of the practice; and what is still worse, to my mind, it undertakes to justify this by associating it with a certain form of charity. In other words, we are endeavouring to give to this petty form of gambling of which I am speaking a virtue that does not inhere in it. The

bill before us introduces this form of gambling, and in order that the habit may become nationwide it provides that the provinces throughout this country may participate. Moreover, the process is to be a continuous one. No period of the year will be free from the spectacle of some part of the country indulging in this form of gambling. Again, it sets one province against another. They enter into competition, and the competition is that one province will be able to extract most money out of the others. It will therefore be a competition between provinces. It will be seen from the provisions of the bill that throughout the year at some time or other one province will be invaded by the others, if its intention is to be carried out.
One of the arguments put forward on behalf of the bill is that we shall be able to go into the United States, a neighbouring country, and there extract from the people, by this particular form of petty gambling, money to be brought here to maintain our Canadian institutions-an obligation which surely is ours as Canadians. Further, and perhaps lastly, the hill undertakes to put the Canadian provinces and Canada as a whole in a competing class with those other countries which have already degraded in this way their forms of raising of money for charitable purposes. Personally I am convinced that the hospitals will not benefit by obtaining money in this manner; it may assist them immediately but in the long run they will be distinctly the losers.
One tiling that was rather curious to me was the attitude taken by the sponsor of the bill the other night. He condemned in very severe terms the method of financing the sale and purchase of wheat, a method which is recognized and has been recognized for years as essential in the handling of this product, recognized by all commission agents on both sides of the water, recognized by farmers who sell the grain, and recognized generally by all those engaged in the handling of it. True, there is an element of uncertainty. There is an undertaking to protect the purchase of wheat against what may happen to it in future sale. We can call that gambling or not, and I am not going to enter into a discussion of that question at the moment. What was anomalous however was that the sponsor of the bill, who condemned that well recognized and well established form of business in this country as in every other country, should now turn round and extol the virtues of this particular form of petty gambling. Truly, he has strained at a gnat and swallowed a camel. For my part I cannot see any virtue in the

bill. I cannot support in any way the raising of money in this manner for any purpose and above all I must refuse to support the raising of money in this way for the assistance of hospitals. In my opinion, as in the opinion of most people who are in closest toudh with hospital administration, it would be detrimental to the cause of these institutions.

Mr. Speaker, there is a point of view in regard to this bill held by very many people in Canada, indeed I think by the majority of the Canadian people. I wish to present that point of view, and I do it more gladly because I believe it is held by the great majority of my own constituents. The sponsor of this bill-I do not know just how serious he was in making the statement-stated that there were many hon. members of this house who would indulge in the practice of gambling if they w^ere not deterred by the fear of being brought before their local churches or exposed in their local newspapers. That to me seems to be an admission that there is a very strong popular sentiment in this country against the principle of this bill. Is it not right tiiat public opinion should prevail in a matter of this kind? Sometimes questions arise in this house upon which a member must judge for himself; sometimes on questions of fact, in connection with which a member has had better opportunity of informing himself than have his constituents, he must assume responsibility for acting according to his own judgment; the time will come when he will have to render to his constituents an account of his stewardship and receive their approval or condemnation. But this bill does not involve a matter of that kind; it is not a question of fact, it is a question involving the well known opinions held by a large number, in fact, as I believe, by the majority of the people of Canada. I believe that this parliament would be violating the trust reposed in it if it endorsed this bill. If there are any members who feel that they are under strong moral compulsion to support the bill; if there are any who feel that to support it is with them a matter of conscience, I have no more to say so far as they are concerned; but I do not think any hon. member will seriously contend that there is any such moral compulsion or that his conscience requires that he should give the measure his endorsation.
I do not intend to discuss the question of private gambling. I have my own personal views on that matter, and my own practice is in harmony with those views. But we should remember that it is not a question of private 53719-255$
gambling that is involved. I am not going to read a lecture to the members of this house, who are adult men and one woman of mature years.
Oh, oh.

I will take back the latter part of my statement. As I say, I am not going to read a lecture to the members of this house, as I do not think it would be my place to do so at this time. I have my own views as to the pernicious effects of even private gambling, but it is not private gambling we are dealing with in this bill. What we have to deal with is the matter of organized or, if you like, commercialized gambling. That is the difference which many people seem to fail to appreciate. It is not a question of making a private bet as to what horse, what hound or what rabbit can run the fastest; the principle involved in this bill is the providing of facilities for people to indulge in the practice of gambling. It is not part of the business of this parliament to provide means for people to indulge in their propensities for gambling. Laws against gambling have been placed upon our statute books because it has been well recognized from the experience gained in the past that the practice was one which affected not only the private lives or morals of men but the public interest. Because it has that effect upon the public wellbeing, this country in common with others has seen fit to pass laws against any organized form of gambling.
For the information of those who say that this is a matter which concerns only the conduct and morals of the private individual, I should like to read an extract from a news item which appeared in the Winnipeg Free Press of April 7. It reads:
Alexander Ramsay Ross, former accountant of the University of Manitoba, was sent to Stony Mountain penitentiary for three years by Magistrate R. M. Noble in provincial police court Thursday.
He pleaded guilty to theft of $14,279.85 _ of the university funds, the defalcations dating back to October, 1931, and continuing to March 21, this year.
In a pica for leniency advanced by C. Tapper, junior, it was pointed out that Ross had given valuable and efficient service to the university since his appointment in 1923, and until the present trouble arose had always borne a good reputation. The real cause of his downfall was "playing the ponies," Mr. Tupper declared. "Legalized race track gambling, and an army of local bookmakers had got the greater part of the stolen money," counsel advised the court.
A further fact stressed was that Ross had received a substantial cut in his salary-it

had been reduced from $4,500 to $3,600 a year -at a time when his client had entered into heavy obligations in connection with the purchase of a home. "Ross always intended to return the money," Mr. Tupper suggested, "but like most others who start to gamble with other people's money-he could never make the 'killing' for which he hoped."
Will anyone say that that is simply a matter of concern to the particular individual involved? Is it simply a private matter that this man should have appropriated over $14,000 of university funds? Surely this action brings it within the realm of matters which concern the public. Our statute books contain a law which legalizes gambling on race tracks by the pari-mutuel system, and in 1923 a proposal to make that practice illegal was voted down by a majority of this house. This parliament must assume a measure of responsibility for the loss incurred to the public by the misappropriation of funds by this young man. It is not simply a matter of private concern, it is a matter of concern to the public when we are to decide whether o>r not we are to organize institutions to enable men to indulge in their passion for gambling.
Now let us turn to the bill itself, on which the hon. member for East Calgary (Mr. Stanley) has made some comments along the lines I had in mind. This bill gives to the attorney general of any province authority to sanction the institution of a sweepstake in that province, but there shall be only one sweepstake in any province in any year. Perhaps those who framed the bill thought they were making a great concession when they said there should be only one sweepstake in any one year, but we can easily see what that would mean. It would simply bring about a succession of sweepstakes, one province vying with the other as to which would get the money. But there is another feature to it. Suppose only one province in the dominion wanted to establish a sweepstake; for instance, let us suppose that the good old province of Ontario had an attorney general who would sanction the promotion of a sweepstake. Let us suppose that every other province was opposed to the idea. In that case you would give to the attorney general of that one province, whether it was Ontario, Manitoba or any other province, the right to foist this institution upon the people of the whole Dominion of Canada. It is provided in the bill that agents shall not be appointed outside the province m which the sweepstake is organized, and I think it is provided also that advertisements for the sweepstake shall not appear in newspapers or magazines that are published outside the province. What does
fMr. Brown.]
that amount to? It is a well known fact that many of our leading newspapers have a dominion-wide circulation, so the fact that agents could not be appointed outside the province and that advertisements could not appear in magazines or papers published outside the province would not prevent these sweepstakes from being advertised over the length and breadth of Canada, and this could be done in spite of any opinions that might be held in eight of the nine provinces. To me that seems a very great weakness in the bill. There is a section in the bill which reads:
Nothing in this act shall prevent the sale outside of Canada by the committee or its agents authorized in writing so to do, of tickets for sweepstakes as authorized to be conducted in accordance with the provisions of this act.
I suppose so far as the sale of tickets outside of Canada is concerned you might as well pass a law trying to prevent the sun from rising to-morrow morning, but I presume the thought was that it should not be illegal to pay money to those outside Canada who might win a prize.
Attracting a little foreign capital.

With regard to attracting foreign capital I am heartily in accord with the sentiments expressed by the hon. member for East Calgary. I think we would be demeaning ourselves if we should say to the people of the United States: "We want to support our hospitals by giving you a chance to win a prize in a sweepstake." It seems to me that would be putting our dominion on a very low level.
I do not think it is necessary for me to take very much time to make clear my sentiments in regard to this matter. The sponsor of the bill made some reference to the Senate and he advanced another argument -though I do not think he could have been altogether serious-to the effect that the majority in the Senate was of necessity composed of wise and experienced gentlemen of high character, and that therefore we should pass the bill also. I am not going to cast any reflections on any member of this house or of any other chamber whose conscience may compel him to support this measure, but in connection with the action of the other house there is one point to which I should like to direct attention. In these days there is a disposition on the part of some to assume that all humane and philanthropic instincts are concentrated in some new party. There is-, a disposition also to assume that all concern

Hospital Sweepstakes
for the moral and economic welfare of the country is located in some new party, I should like to point out, because I think it is worth pointing out to the people of Canada, that the leaders of both parties in the other house opposed this bill. I am happy to believe that if this matter should come to a division in this house it will be opposed by the leader of the government and by the leader of the official opposition, no matter what the other parties may do. I think it desirable that this condition of affairs should be called to the attention of the country, and I am happy to do so at this time. We cannot afford to altogether ignore the higher principles which govern men in their relations one to another when we are dealing with these things in parliament. The Prime Minister himself has recognized that fact, and in a splendid speech a few days ago the right hon. leader of the opposition recognized the need of giving attention to some of those things which move men to action. A short time ago the former minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Malcolm) used these words:
I am firmly convinced that the greatest trouble facing the world to-day is the result of a narrow spirit of selfishness, the constant thinking of monetary interests. In every dispute that arises, in every debate, economics are being placed ahead of humanity.
I should like to quote also the report of an incident that took place in the British House of Commons not so very long ago, when Mr. George Lansbury, leader of the Labour opposition, put to the House of Commons his party's latest vote of censure on the government on the score of the government's failure to deal with unemployment:
With trembling voice the old warrior of labour addressed the house in these terms: "This old world is in its present condition because we have all been living the wrong way. We thought that we did the best for ourselves by only thinking of ourselves. We believed that the aim of life was what we got and not what we gave. I believe that the British parliament and the British nation, if they really believe in the gospel and in doing to others as they would be done unto, could lead the world in a new campaign. We can do it if we have the will, but it must be done on the basis of working in the service of one another, and none of us asking from the world more than we are prepared, according to our ability, to give back to the world.
That is a very striking phrase which might be used in connection with this bill. Mr. Stanley Baldwin, Conservative ex-Prime Minister, replying for the government, said:
I am sure that the right hon. gentleman need make lio apology to the house for the concluding words of his speech. I know that they will find 'in echo in many hearts throughout the house.
Perhaps with these examples before us, Mr. Speaker, I may 'be excused if I appeal to the members of this house to take cognizance of those things which have their effect upon human life and which play a part in developing humanity to the highest level. It would be my earnest hope, Mr. Speaker, that this house might defeat this bill without a division.

Mr. Speaker, before the bill passes I should like to offer a few comments. In the first place, I do not think we are going to make angels by legislation. People gamble anyway, whether you legalize it or not. It is a gamble when we come into this world; it is a gamble when every member of this house presents himself before the electors, and when you go out of this world that is the most serious gamble of all.
I am very sorry, Mr. Speaker, to have to disagree with my hon. friend from Lisgar (Mr. Brown) for the first time since 1921, but I do so sincerely. I like taking a chance myself, and I do take a chance. I would ask, is there any member of this house who does not take a chance? We all do it, and we have to do it to carry on our everyday activities. If any hon. member wishes to tell me that he has never taken a chance, a gambling chance, if you like, I shall sit down and be glad to hear from him.
I remember many years ago when prohibition was the cry in this country, and what happened? Finally every province followed the old province of Quebec in putting prohibition legislation on its statute books. The provincial governments went into the liquor business themselves, and began making profits, and the result was that the taxpayer who did not drink had his taxes reduced although he did not save very much more by that. But every province has gone into the liquor business and is benefiting to the extent of millions and millions; of dollars, which is used in order to reduce taxes.
Would the hon. member name one province in which the taxes have been reduced?
What did you do with the profits that the province of Ontario made?
Where is the province that has reduced its taxes?

If you did not have that profit you would have to increase your taxes; that is only natural. I think the Canadian people are prepared to take advantage of the millions and millions of dollars made from the sale of liquor. Then why should I not

Hear, hear.

There is evil in gambling, yes; there is evil in drinking; there is evil in many other things that we do; but gambling exists, and I am in favour of this bill. Whether it is framed exactly as I should like I do not know. I venture to say that there are many members of parliament who have sweepstakes tickets in their pockets right now. Undoubtedly gambling exists; then why not control it to a certain degree? Do not brand people as criminals because they take a chance; for they will take it anyway. There are many people in this country to-day who are in favour of sweepstakes. There are many who feel that many of our charitable institutions and hospitals, which the hon. member for East Calgary mentioned, are not going to be able to continue to function unless they find some means of raising funds. Will my hon. friend from East Calgary undertake to find people who will contribute to keep our hospitals going? I read in the papeTs only to-day that the free clinic, one of the most important branches of the general hospital in Winnipeg, is closing because of lack of funds. That clinic is saving life after life with its free treatment to the people of the city of Winnipeg, but those people will be deprived of that clinic unless money is forthcoming from some place.

Do -not let us 'be hypocrites. Let us be frank. We gamble. Let us control it. Let the people take a chance, and let it be legal for them to do so, because they will take a chance anyway. I intend to support this bill.

I assure the house at the outset that I Ch-all not speak long. I do not see why we have not had a vote on this question long ago. It is my desire, in case the predictions of an hon. member come true and we decide this question without a vote, to show now which side I am on. First, I am against this bill, and for several reasons. I entirely disagree with the principle. Secondly, I am glad to have the opportunity of voting with my opponents across the floor, for it is very seldom indeed that I get the opportunity. I am prouder than ever of this house to think, rightly I believe, that -the leaders of 'the three groups in this house are against .this bill. I know the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) dropped a -hint some time ago that he was against it; I know -that my own leader is against it, and I believe that the leader of the group to my left is against the bill also. It is a rare occasion for me to have the privilege of voting with all three, and I want to embrace that opportunity, in addition to opposing this bill on general principles.
I am not going to pass any strictures on the source from which this bill came, or on its sponsor who introduced it into this house excellently, from his viewpoint-and I think be -believes in what he said-or on the other chamber, except to remark -that had that noble old character, the laite Sir George E. Foster, been still with us, this bill would not be here to-night. He was always on the side of beneficent social legislation such as this bill decidedly is not.
My hon. friend from Provencher (Mr. Beaubien) rather startled me. Gambling will 'be with us anyway, he said. Well, murder will be with us, and has been with us ever since Cain slew Abel. Shall we therefore legalize murder? Stealing and perjury have been with us ever since the days of Ananias and Sapphira. Shall we therefore legalize these atrocities? I know my hon'. friend from Provencher does not mean what he says when in effect, he talks in that way. He was good enough to say that this is the first occasion upon which he has disagreed with the hon. member for Lisgar. Surely he made an unfortunate choice when he decided to disagree on a -measure of this kind.
I should like to comment in regard to the unavoidable partnership of gamblers and

Hospital Sweepstakes
hospitals, as it appears in. the bill, a circumstance which is most objectionable to me. For many years at was my privilege to administer the hospitals and public health of the province of Saskatchewan. Naturally for that reason I became keenly interested in hospitals. To my surprise I learned during those years that many men and women who took veiy little interest in other philanthropic or church work were intensely devoted to and interested in the maintenance of hospitals. It is a type of work which appealed strongly to some people, in fact to the extent that it almost became their religion. I am afraid if we associate with those people others who secure money in this questionable fashion we will to a very substantial extent dry up that beneficent source of revenue.
I believe we should encourage the promotion of individual giving towards hospitals. Those who have never been in a hospital is indeed in one respect most fortunate, but they have missed some valuable lessons which can be learned only in hospitals. Doubtless some have not learned the joy of giving towards those who are less fortunate and find themselves sick in hospital afflicted with one sort of ailment or another. Therefore I am of the opinion that anything which will discourage philanthropic and free giving towards hospitals should be frowned upon.
I have another reason for objecting to the bill. On a former occasion in this house I made the mistake of voting for a relatively harmless proposition. I believe it was not as bad as this one, but inasmuch as I had the example of the Churches to follow I thought I was quite safe in voting for the introduction of a mild form of gambling into our exhibition associations.
You introduced it.

No, it was in the criminal code, and was under the supervision of the Minister of Justice. I supported this relatively harmless measure, and now for the first time I wish to make public the recantation of my attitude taken at that time. In those days I was younger and less guarded, and like the hon. members for Provencher (Mr. Beaubien) and Quebec South (Mr. Power) have done now, I made a mistake. For reasons which I shall not enumerate I am not now going to repeat that mistake. I should be much happier to support a restrictive measure against gambling than the one now before the house. Of all times under the sun
to open up and increase facilities for gambling, this is the worst I can imagine.
Undoubtedly there are many hon. members in the house who are not averse to gambling, who may not be averse even to this type of gambling, which is pure chance. Perhaps in normal times they would support the measure before us. However I believe their best judgment will tell them that the excessive spirit of gambling and chance during the last twenty or twenty-five years is one of the reasons why people in Canada and in other parts of the world find themselves faced with the ghastly depression in which we are now weltering and wallowing, and from which God only knows when we will recover. Surely to increase facilities for gambling would at this time particularly be nothing short of a crime.
I submit my views to the house without any intention of offending, and without criticizing any hon. member whose views may be different. However I feel that if we in this chamber opened up further channels for gambling the electors of Canada would think we had gone plumb bughouse. This is not a matter of speculating on the wheat pit. A man well versed in market conditions has some knowledge of world prices of wheat, and general conditions, and his knowledge and skill stands him in good stead. But when we have something that is a pure game of chance, a lottery, at which any kind of dub can make a lucky try, we have the most vicious and objectionable type of gambling.
Then, in regard to the man who gambles on race horses, I could make a few comments. By the way, that matter came to my notice in the Department of Agriculture and has been a legacy bestowed upon every minister for some time back. If a man has some knowledge of horses, information concerning the owners and jockeys, and knows that they will not sell him out, he has a better chance of winning. Therefore skill and expert knowledge of horses may help him.

They only think they
know.

This legislation involves nothing but pure chance, a shaking of the dice, a lottery. Of course we realize there is chance in horse racing, but we must admit that knowledge of good horses, information as to their records and previous performances, and the honesty of the owner and jockey, give one a chance of winning.

Especially if you have a
dupe book with you.

I do not pretend
to know all about it, but I am familiar with some phases of the matter. I do know that one most capable man in the Department of Agriculture went to the terrible bow-wows largely as a result of gambling while administering the aet. I do not believe the virus permeated my being at all, but there is a chance of younger men being affected. Consequently without further ado I wish to ally myself with those hon. members who have spoken against the bill, and with the leaders in the house-if I surmise correctly that they are all against the measure. I shall vote with great joy against any bill of this nature, and against any attempt deliberately and by our own hands and voices to increase the facilities for gambling at this critical period in our economic history.

Mr. Speaker, I intend to detain the house only two or three minutes. Possibly my position in regard to this bill is the most difficult experienced by any hon. member, because I find from the report of what transpired in another place that my constituency voted by five to one in favour of a measure similar to the one now before us. Therefore it is a question whether my duty as a member from a Canadian city should come into conflict with my own judgment.
With the indulgence of the house I shall inflict upon hon. members two short quotations from Burke's famous speech to the electors of Bristol. Possibly from his remarks on that great occasion I may find a reconciliation between my judgment and what might be construed to be my duty. He said:
Certainly, gentlemen, it ought to be the happiness and glory of a representative to live m the strictest union, the closest correspondence, and the most unreserved communication with his constituents. Their wishes ouo-ht to have great weight with him; their opinion high respect; their business unremitted attention. It is_ his duty to sacrifice his repose, his pleasures his satisfactions, to theirs; and above all, ever' and in all cases, to prefer their interest 'to his ?wm But, his unbiased opinion, his mature judgment, his enlightened conscience, he ought not to sacrifice to you; to any man, or to any set of men living. These he does not derive from your pleasure; no. nor from the law and the constitution. They are a trust from Providence, for the abuse of which lie is deeply answerable. Your representative owes you not his industry only, but his judgment: and he betrays, instead of serving you, if he sacrifices it to your opinion.
Again the second quotation is:
Parliament is not a congress of ambassadors from diflerent and hostile interests; -which interests each must maintain, as an agent and advocate, against other agents and advocates; 
but parliament is a deliberative assembly of one nation, with one interest, that of the whole; where, not local purposes, not local prejudices ought to guide, but the general good, resulting from the general reason of the whole. You choose a member indeed; but when you have chosen him, he is not member of Bristol, but lie is a member of parliament. If the local constituent should have an interest, or should form an hasty opinion, evidently opposite to the real good of the rest of the community, the member for that place ought to be as far. as any other, from any endeavour to give it effect.
And so, Mr. Speaker, although my riding has voted in support of a measure similar to this by a majority of five to one, my judgment compels me to vote against it.

speechtext:
I will not detain the house very
long, I think almost everything has been said that it is necessary to say. I am opposed to the principle underlying this bill, because it seems to me that gambling is essentially the idea of getting something for nothing, and I take it that at this time above all others we ought not to encourage that spirit in the people. However, I must say that I cannot get up any very great enthusiasm about voting against the bill, simply because there are on the statute books other pieces of legislation which legalize gambling. There are in practice a great many institutions carrying on a species of gambling. In the business world we have our real estate exchanges and grain exchanges and stock exchanges, on which there is practised what is in my judgment virtually gambling. Therefore it seems to me ridiculous that we should go after the little man, perhaps the poor Chinaman who plays a game of fan tan, and these larger and much more dangerous forms of gambling should go on unchecked.

You are
in favour of it?

No, but I say I am almost tempted, on account of the general injustice of the thing, to vote in favour of it. Sometimes one .is tempted to do that. On the other hand, if one votes in favour of this particular measure it means the extension of the area, and the creation of a certain sort of vested interest that makes it much more to fight against the general evil. So while I protest very decidedly against the discrimination involved in voting down one particular kind of gambling alone, while this house is making no effort whatever to get rid of other types of gambling that are much more serious, at the same time in view of the considerations I have outlined I feel that I must vote against the bill.

1 he house resumed consideration in committee of Bill No. 37, respecting the Canadian National Railways and to provide for cooperation with the Canadian Pacific railway system and for other purposes-Mr. Manion.- Mr. Gagnon in the chair.

When the house rose at six o'clock I was making a few remarks with regard to an amendment which I proposed to offer to subsection 1 of section 4 of the bill. I had just pointed out that when the Drayton-Acworth commission sat in 1917 they had also, as did the Duff commission, recommended that trustees be appointed to administer the national railway system. Clause No. 31 in the 1917 report of the royal commission on railways and transportation recommended that there be five trustees and that these be named in the legislation. I had pointed out that, as the Prime Minister himself had said, if this railway were a private company it would be treated as though it were in liquidation, and as the bonds of this public company were guaranteed by the dominion it was advisable to appoint trustees to administer the affairs of the railway. I had further said that if the trustees were to be appointed, the House of Commons, representing, as the members do, the shareholders of the system, should be the body to appoint the trustees, or a receiver or liquidator, or whatever term we chose to apply to these three men to whom we were giving full charge of the system.
The legislation provides two things that remove from those who are to administer the system much of the responsibility. First of all it removes the financial difficulties, because it provides that any deficits that occur are to be met out of the public treasury. I suggested to the Minister of Railways that in selecting the chairman of the board of trustees, it would appear advisable that he should select
C.N.R.-C.P.R. Bill

the most able railway administrator he could secure on the continent, for the reason that if success is to come to the railway system all that can be expected of the board of trustees is efficient and economical management. The financial problem is being handled by the Minister of Finance of this dominion.

Secondly, the success of the system will be predicated very largely upon the policies of the government of Canada. We all realize, whether we wish to blame it on the government in power in this country or on governments in power in other countries, that restrictive trade policies the world over have done much to diminish tonnage not only of railways but of ocean shipping companies. Such policies have done much to decrease the volume of business transacted. The men appointed by the government to administer the policies of the railway will have nothing whatever to do with the policies of the government, and any deficits that occur will be provided for by the Minister of Finance.
My suggestion therefore, and it is only a suggestion, is that the chairman of the board should be a railway operator. If the government is prepared to consider the advisability of sharing with other members of the House of Commons the responsibility for the appointment of trustees, so that it can truthfully be said-what the Prime Minister indicated-* that the object is to remove as far as possible any accusation of political partisanship. I believe that the amendment which I propose to submit would free the government from the possibilities of any such charge. If the government could decide upon the men it desired, the amendment could be offered at such time as the minister was prepared to make the selection. The section now reads:
The governor in council may vacate all nominations heretofore made to the board of directors of the national company pursuant to section 3 of the national act-
That means that they may dismiss existing directors.
-and may appoint in the place and stead of and in succession to the incorporators of that company three trustees whose powers, rights, privileges, immunities, duties, responsibilities and restrictions shall be as in and by this act provided.

My amendment is to strike out the word "may" in line 28 and substitute the word "shall", and to strike out all of lines 31 and 32 and substitute therefor the words, " and hereby appoint as trustees the following". The amendment would therefore read: That section 4 of part I be amended by striking out the word "may" in line 28 and substituting therefor the word "shall", and by striking out all the words in lines 31 and 32 and substituting therefor the words, "and hereby appoint as trustees the following". I have left the lines blank. I do not know whether, in submitting an amendment, it would be in order to insert names; I do not presume to submit names to the government. If the minister thinks that he can accept such an amendment I will submit it; otherwise I propose to let the matter stand. I leave it to him whether I shall submit it or not.

I know that the hon. gentleman offers the amendment in the best of good faith and I have every respect for his submission. At the same time there are a number of reasons why the amendment cannot be accepted. Let me deal with a few of the suggestions my hon. friend has offered. In the first place, as regards substituting the word "shall" for the word "may", I understand that it has adways been the custom to use the word "may" with respect to the governor in council. That is a small matter, but I just mention it in passing. In that case, generally speaking, the word "may" means "shall".
_ Another point made by the hon. gentleman was that the chairman of the board of trustees should be a first class railway operator. In passing may I point out that at the present time we have not only one but a number of good railway operators connected with the Canadian National Railways. I have heard the most complimentary references made to Mr. Ilungerford and the other officers of the railways and I submit that the splendid work which they have done in the past indicates conclusively that they are capable of operating the railway in excellent manner. My own opinion-I am expressing this just the same as the hon. gentleman expressed his opinion- is that rather than a railway operator, what we need is someone who will be competent to supervise the general policies of the road. Without meaning to be critical of the past, I believe that had there been greater supervision from the financial standpoint of the management and the capital expenditures of the road, it would have been better. The hon. gentleman also suggested that we should choose someone from this continent. Without attempting to make any political capital out of the

C.N.R.-C.P.R. Bill
reference of my hon, friend, may I say that my feeling is that if possible, and I think it is possible, we should obtain a man from this country. I have no desire to reflect upon the suggestion made by the hon. gentleman that these men should be named in the bill itself, but there are two reasons why I do not think that would be possible. The first is that the bill is not yet law, and the second is that when the bill was introduced both the Prime Minister and myself took the attitude that we would be ready to consider amendments suggested by hon. members. I think we have proven our good faith by submitting two amendments along the lines suggested by hon, gentlemen opposite. Until the bill is law and we know its terms, we could not very well approach outstanding men in Canada with a view to asking them to take this position. We would first have to know that the position was created and we would also require the general support and advice of the House of Commons as a whole. In view of these considerations it is not possible for the government at the moment to indicate just who should be appointed to these positions. I make that statement quite frankly and because of these facts the suggestion which my hon. friend has made, in good faith I know, is not acceptable to the government at the present time.

Mr. Chairman, the former Minister of Labour, the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Heenan) had an amendment which he intended to offer. He has been unavoidably prevented from being here to-day, and, as a former Minister of Labour, not as leader of the opposition, I should like to move an amendment which indicates views which I very strongly entertain. It is my opinion that at least one member of the board of trustees should be a person who would be regarded as representing labour upon that board, whether the board be made up of three, five or whatever other number of members may be decided upon. It will be for the government to decide just how many members shall compose this board, but I believe that, at this time, when industry the world over is undergoing a change, and when there is a very strong feeling against monopoly of control on the part of capital of great industrial enterprises, every effort should be made by a representative body such as this house to see that the classes immediately and mostly affected in industry are accorded a voice in the formation of industrial policy. I know it will be argued that, because this board may have the unpleasant duty of cutting down services, causing the number of men employed to be reduced, and possibly reducing wages and the like, it would be inadvisable to have someone possessing the confidence of labour upon the board. From my point of view, the reasons I have just mentioned are the strongest that could be advanced for having someone in the confidence of railway labour upon this board. I believe that working men are quite as reasonable as any other class in the community, when it comes to what relates to conditions of employment much more reasonable in fact, than are any of the others who have to do with the shaping of working conditions. I believe that the whole railway policy would be carried out in a finer spirit if organized labour were represented on the board which was to determine that policy. Being given information with respect to the extent and nature of business the world over, and other like considerations, the representative of labour upon the board of trustees would be able to form an intelligent view of the situation in a better manner than would foe possible in any other way. His support of any measure which involved a reduction of wages, the lessening of staff or matters of a similar nature, would carry considerable weight with the great body of railway employees. Whether the board is to be composed of three of five members, as the bill now stands, a majority, which must include the chairman, is required in order to have any decision of the board prevail. In these circumstances, there would always be at least two members who may very properly be regarded as representing the capital investors and the community generally, and, for that reason, the interests of investors or the public generally would be in no danger of being sacrificed at the hands of the one representative commanding the confidence of labour.
I should like to mention to the committee that it was the Drayton-Acworth commission which made originally the recommendation that there should be a board of trustees. I think they recommended that this board should consist of five members, but whatever the number they certainly recommended that there should be one trustee selected as especially possessing the confidence of the railway employees. That commission was appointed by hon. gentlemen opposite, it was appointed by the government of the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen. It heard evidence from all parties and came to the conclusion that, whatever the number of trustees might be, one should 'be selected as especially possessing the confidence of the railway employees. I am not submitting that this representative should necessarily be a railway employee, to be chosen from the ranks of the
C.N.R.-C.P.R. Bill

employees of the railway. I am following the exact wording of the Dray ton-Aeworth recommendation.
Another reason for making su-ch an appointment is the fact 'that ait the present time labour is represented upon the board of directors. As hon. members know, the president of the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada is one of the directors of the Canadian National Railways, he having been appointed by the late Liberal administration and continued as a director by the present administration. I venture to say that if the directors appointed by the present administration or those appointed by the previous administration, or the officers of the railway were asked whether Mr. Tom Moore had been helpful or otherwise as a director, the answer most emphatically would be that his services had been of great value to all who are concerned with the management of the railway and the shaping of its policies. It seems to me that, having established the precedent of giving labour representation upon the board of directors, it would, apart from all else, be a great mistake to take a backward step by now doing away with that representation.
I would urge further that in these matters the government ought to set an example to industry generally. I do not think representation by someone commanding the confidence of railway employees should be confined to the national system; I believe the Canadian Pacific might well adopt a similar policy in respect to its board of directors and that all large industries might well do the same. I believe also that, if industry does not do so it will be all the worse for the investors in the long run. If there is not a natural evolution by the gradual broadening of the representation of all classes immediately concerned in industry on the boards that control industrial policies, there is nothing left but a kind of action which would not commend itself to any deliberative body such as this.
Furthermore, in railway matters it is allimportant to have good-will and a good spirit prevailing throughout the system. There is nothing that can more effectually impede the satisfactory working of a railway than a lack of confidence on the part of the employees with respect to the policies by which they are governed. In that regard I believe that the railway as a financial institution will be benefited materially if labour is given representation on the board.
In conclusion may I say that I regard labour as a partner with capital in all industrial enterprise; certainly in railway enterprise labour is an essential partner. May I point out that our railways employ larger numbers of men

than most of our industries, and that men who enter railway service as a rule go into it for life. They invest their lives in that form of service, but they invest them again in a way even more immediate. Railroading is a hazardous buiness; there is not a man who goes out on a train who does not from that moment to the end of his journey take his life in his hands and all that his life means in the home from which he comes. Men who are giving their lives to industrial service in that immediate way ought to be represented on any board of trustees or directors which has to do with fashioning the policies under which they are obliged to work. So, Mr. Chairman, I would move that section 4 be amended by adding after the word "trustees" in line 32 the words:
-one selected as especially possessing the confidence of railway employees.
I hope the minister will find it possible to accept that amendment.

I shall not traverse the ground covered by the right hon. gentleman, because the question was discussed in a very general way on the second reading of the bill. At that time, however, I did point out-we were dealing with the Duff commission, but I think the same observation applies to the appointment of trustees-that it is a little difficult to choose a representative of one class without remembering other classes who are affected also to a great extent by our railways, notably the agricultural class. For example, I pointed out that at the peak there are not more than 200,000 men employed on all the railways of Canada whereas there are more than a million agricultural workers in this dominion, including farmers and workers on farms. As the agriculturist is affected in his purchases by a tax, that is, a freight rate, on practically everything he buys, he also is very greatly affected by the operation of the railways. If class representation is to be given on a small board of trustees such as this the agriculturist might well and justly take the attitude that he also has a right to representation on the board.
I merely mention this as one difficulty which might arise. There is another point, however; it is that the Canadian National Railways Act itself contained no clause providing that labour should be represented on the board, though as a matter of fact the governments of the past all appointed someone as representing labour, as my right hon. friend has said. I submit that a matter of this kind should be left for decision to the government appointing the trustees, and that their hands should not be tied by such an amendment. In

other words, I believe the government should be left as untrammelled in carrying out this act as other governments were left in the carrying out of the Canadian National Railways Act, to which as a matter of fact Part I of the present act is an amendment. So I do not believe the committee would be wise to accept the amendment proposed by the right hon. gentleman. There may be other reasons that could be advanced but those happen to come to my mind at the moment.

I very much regret the attitude taken by the Minister of Railways with regard to this amendment. Even though he could not accept it I think at least he might have given it a little more sympathetic consideration than he appeared to give in his reply. The hon. gentleman tried to justify his position by the fact that there was no representative of labour on the Duff commission.

Nor of agriculture.
Mr. HEAPS'. I think that was one of the regrettable features of the Duff commission. There was distinct class representation in that commission; that was evidenced by the minister's remarks when he introduced this measure dealing with our railway problem. At that time the minister said that the two appointees, the one from the United States and the other from Great Britain, had been placed on this commission in order to give confidence to those holding the securities of the two railway companies If that is not class representation I do not know what it is.

I corrected that later on; I said these men were not appointed as class representatives. They were appointed to give confidence to those people in the two countries holding bonds and securities to the value of hundreds of millions of dollars, but they were not put on as representatives of those people.

They were appointed in order to give confidence to the bondholders in those countries. A representative of labour on that commission might have given just as much satisfaction to our own people, and I think the government of the day should have been just as much concerned in giving satisfaction to our own people as in giving satisfaction to people living in other parts of the world. This evening the Minister of Railways said that he hoped in some way to go back on that former attitude of the government and that when the board is appointed the government will not go beyond the confines of this dominion in selecting them. I am in hearty agreement with that attitude, and I wish that it had been adopted in regard to the Duff commission itself, instead of appointing two gentlemen from outside of this country for the express purpose, in my estimation of recommending that we do something which they found it impossible to do themselves, for I see in to-day's papers that the Delaware and Hudson Railway, of which Mr. Loree is president, is in somewhat the same position as the Canadian National Railways. Yet this same gentleman comes to us to tell us how to settle our railway problem when he is not in a position to settle his own.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I think his road paid a dividend last year.

To-day's papers report a loss of $45,000,000 for the road.
In 1927 at the Conservative party convention held in Winnipeg a plank was written into their platform in favour of giving labour representation on these commissions appointed
C.N.R.-CP.R. Bill

by the government. I am sure that the Minister of Railways is not going to go back on that plank which was adopted at the Winnipeg convention only a few short years ago. I hope that that recommendation was something more than mere window dressing. The workers on the railways will be very much disappointed at the attitude adopted by the Minister of Railways this evening when he does not hold out any hopes, in my estimation, of giving labour representation on the board of trustees, which will have control to a very large extent of the railways and will have some say as to the conditions under which railway men shall work.

The hon. gentleman has no right to say that I held out no hope whatsoever. I said that the government should not have its hands tied in regard to this matter. Speaking of window dressing, may I with all respect suggest to my hon. friend that there is no group in this house who do so much window dressing as he and his friends. Their whole attitude here and everywhere is one of window dressing, appealing to class all the time. That is the attitude my hon. friend is taking now. Not only in this house but on the hustings the whole attitude of that party is one of appealing to class, of setting class against class, so when it comes to window dressing I think I might learn a lot from my hon. friend. As regards the remark of the leader of the opposition in regard to the danger to life of the railway men themselves when running a train, that is true, but the passenger on the train also runs a considerable risk.
But the passenger is on the train one day, while the railway man is on the year around.

My deputy points out that there are more accidents on the highways than on the railways, and I believe he is right although I have not the figures at hand. I do not think the government's hands should be tied in regard to matters of this kind. When the appointment of the trustees takes place the matter will have to be considered by the government and the responsibility taken by the government. The door is not shut by any means. The question will have to be considered from all angles. It has not been considered as yet, I say quite frankly.
Amendment (Mr. Mackenzie King) negatived.
Subsection 1 of section 4 agreed to.
On section 4, subsection 2-Chairman.

This subsection provides that one of the trustees shall be chairman and shall devote his whole time to the per-

formance of the duties of his office, and shall not be an officer of any company other than a company which is comprised in the national railways. I wish to submit to the committee an amendment to answer the suggestion made there that one of the trustees only, the chairman, shall devote his whole time to the performance of the duties of his office. The implication is that he alone of the trustees shall devote his full time to the duties of his office. I submit that with the amount of money that the people of this country have invested in these railways, their immense importance and the service that they give to the people, if the board is to be limited to three trustees they should not only be the best men obtainable but all three trustees should give their whole time to the work. The Canadian National Railways Act provided that there should be from five to fifteen directors, and actually I think there were seventeen directors, and seventeen I think for the Canadian Pacific. Now, when the number is being limited to three, I submit not only that they should be the most capable men who can be obtained but that they should give their full time to the work. I do not know that there is any great object in taking up too much of the time of the committee in discussing this matter, as there are other matters to be discussed, and I therefore move that subclause 2 of section 4 be amended by striking it out and substituting therefor the following:
One of such trustees shall be the chairman Each trustee shall devote his whole time to the performance of the duties of his office and shall not be an officer of any company other than a company which is comprised in national railways, and shall not during his tenure of office as trustee become a director of any company other than a company which is comprised in national railways of Which he was not a director at the time of his appointment.

I *would suggest that subclause 2 of clause 4 stand with the amendment which has just been proposed, on the ground that this is a question which we think is worthy of consideration. The Prime Minister this afternoon, speaking on this very question, mentioned that he thought it might be well that the three trustees for the first year at any rate give their entire time to the work. In view of that and my hon. friend's remarks I would therefore suggest that the subclause stand with the amendment which has been moved, and we will come back to it probably to-morrow, in the meantime giving further consideration to it. It might be advisable that for the first year, or possibly longer,

C.N.R.-C.P.R. Bill
the three trustees should give their full time to the work, and so, Mr, Chairman, I propose that this subclause stand and that we proceed with the bill.
Has the government decided to maintain only three trustees?-because I find a great deal of opinion in favour of five.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: We intend to stick to three.
Why should there be discrimination against the individual who is at present or who formerly held a position of director?
Why any discrimination against a present director?
Yes.

There is no discrimination against them. I have put myself on record here and elsewhere in regard to the splendid work they have done. However there is an opinion that there should be three trustees in charge of the road; there is no discrimination being shown.
Under the bill as drafted a director of the Canadian Pacific Railway could be appointed, but he could not become a director after he was appointed.
He will not be appointed.

The minister might add the word "director" the first time the word "officer" is used, to make the correction that is necessary. He might be a director of the Canadian Pacific Railway and still be appointed, but he could not become a director after he was appointed.

The minister should put in some phraseology which would indicate that upon becoming a trustee a man should resign his directorship in other companies, because there is nothing to prevent his retaining his directorship in other companies. There is, however, something to prevent his becoming a director after he has become a trustee.
He could not be an officer, but he could be a director of any company when he was appointed.

I should like to call the attention of the minister to that part of clause 2 section 4 which reads, "and shall not be an officer of any company." As I take it, an officer is a paid servant, other than a director. There is no provision saying that he shall not be a director. It should read, "and shall not be an officer or director of any company."

We had intended moving an amendment to that clause. The Minister of Public Works had it before him, but in view of the amendment of the hon. member for West Middlesex (Mr. Elliott) I thought perhaps we could leave it until we had decided upon that point. I shall take up the suggestion now made regarding a director of the Canadian Pacific Railway and see how it fits in. I suggest that the clause stand, and that we proceed with clause 5.

Subsection 2 of clause 4 will stand.
On section 5, subsection 1-Salaries.

Subsection 1 of section 5 reads:
The trustees shall be paid by the national company such salaries as may from time to time be fixed by the governor in council, and if any trustee is in receipt of a pension from any railway company he shall not be entitled to receive or to be paid such pension during his term of office.
I should like to follow that section by an amendment to the effect that the trustees of the national company shall be paid by parliament out of the yearly estimates. I submit that is the only way we can have control over the trustees. Personally my great objection to the bill is that essentially it is an emergency measure to deal with an emergent situation. We are making the persons to whom the operation of the act is to be entrusted practically irrevocable directors, and unless some control is retained by parliament I believe we will defeat the intention of the Canadian people. As the section reads the trustees shall be entitled to be paid from the earnings of the road. They need not come to parliament for their saLaries, and are not responsible to parliament in any way. If an amendment were moved along these lines, namely by striking out the words, " national company " in the first line and substituting therefor the words, " out of moneys voted by parliament in the annual estimates " I suggest that then the conduct and administration would be subject to the control of the shareholders who, after all, are the members of parliament representing the people of Canada, the owners of the road.
Is that an amendment?
Yes.

In the first place I suggest that the amendment is out of order, because it would be putting charges upon the parliament of Canada, something a private member cannot do. It would be placing upon the parliament of Canada the necessity of paying

C.N.R.-CP.R. Bill
the trustees. However I merely mention that objection; the chairman may consider the amendment and give his ruling thereon.
The hon. member stated that the trustees are not in any way subject to the control of parliament. I do not agree with him, because if he will look at section 12 he will find the following:
The annual budget of the national railways shall be under the control of the trustees. Amounts required for income deficits, for interest on obligations outstanding in the hands of the public, for capital expenditures and for refunding or retirement of maturing securities shall be submitted by the trustees to the Minister of Finance for the consideration of the governor in council prior to presentation to parliament. Income deficits shall not be funded.
That clause includes practically every need of the Canadian National Railways, and to my mind by that clause the parliament of Canada will have just as much opportunity as it has to-day, if it so chooses, to investigate the expenditures of the national railways. That is the way it strikes me. Then section 14 provides the annual report must be made to parliament. It states:
The trustees shall make a report annually to parliament setting forth in a summary manner the results of their operations, any cooperative measures. plans or arrangements effected pursuant to this act,-
And so on. Those two clauses make them subject to parliament. To my mind those two clauses make them responsible to parliament.
No.
We are not dealing with section 12, but the minister has referred to it. I should like to be assured as to whether or not parliament has any control over the receipts of the road.

Not the
slightest.

After all,
that is the main source from which the trustees will operate-the revenues of the road.
They have no control over the receipts, perhaps, but when they come to parliament under section 12 and ask for money-
For specific purposes.
But those specific purposes cover all the needs of the railroad.

No.
[Mr Manion.]

If the section means that the revenues of the road come under review, then of course the minister is correct. But if not, if we are merely to vote deficits and capital requirements, then we have no control over the trustees at all.

There are only three purposes for which they may come to parliament, -first, to get amounts required for income deficits, secondly for interest on obligations outstanding in the hands of the public, and third for capital expenditures and for refunding or retirement of maturing securities. Those matters shall be submitted by the trustees to the Minister of Finance for the consideration of the governor in council, prior to presentation to parliament. The section is not quite clear as to whether or not they have to come to parliament. The statement is made that the Minister of Finance reviews the amounts required. This may be only a formal presentation, and we may be told now, as we have been told for years

and I am not blaming the minister particularly-that it is not in the public interest to give out the information. The trustees are representing the people of Canada. We should have some kind of control over their actions, and I submit the only control we can have is by voting their salaries.

If the hon. gentleman will permit me to deal with section 12, it seems to me that section covers practically everything. For example, amounts required for income deficits, that is the difference between the net operating income of the railway and the interest owing to the public on the bonds of the railway-
The time might come when there will be no deficits.

If the time ever comes
when the Canadian National Railways will require no assistance for income deficits, it seems to me that would be an ideal condition for the Canadian National Railways to reach, and it would then be well for this parliament to keep out of the business and let the management operate the road without any interference.
But to get back to my argument, I say that the provision for looking into the cause of the deficit would cover practically every branch of the railroad's affairs. True, as to certain information being given to parliament, I presume whatever government is in power would take the same attitude as has been taken in the past; there is certain information that the railway management say it is not in

C.N.R.-C.PJI. Bill
the railway's interest and therefore not in the public interest to divulge. I presume the same attitude will be taken in the future. But the section also refers to amounts required for interest on obligations outstanding in the hands of the public, for capital expenditures, and for refunding or retirement of maturing securities. To my mind that covers every possible branch of the railway's affairs, and the parliament of Canada will have it in its power to go into these details as far as they ever have in the past; with this exception, recommended by the Duff commission, that the officers of the railway should not be brought before the parliamentary committee. But that is no reason why we should not bring the trustees before the committee and have them give a report.
Then section 14:
The trustees shall make a report annually to parliament setting forth in _ a summary manner the results of their operations . . .
That would deal with the same question. I submit in all seriousness and sincerity that to my mind, as far as parliament wishes to control the financial arrangements of the railway, it has all power to do so under sections 12 and 14.

Taking the minister's own
argument, as to these matters which he says come under the control of parliament-which argument I am not prepared to admit-they are income deficits, interest on obligations in the hands of the public, capital expenditures, and retirement of maturing securities. Not one of those things do we dare refuse to vote. It is pointed out to me that in the first paragraph it is provided that the annual budget of the national railways shall be under the control of the trustees. We dare not refuse to vote the income deficits; we dare not refuse to vote the interest on obligations in the hands of the public, for if we do the road is bankrupt, and if so the country is bankrupt,-
Is not that true at this moment just as it will be in the future? But we do look into the accounts.

But if we have the trustees here before us having their salaries voted, we can criticize them. As representing the people who own the road, the shareholders of the road, we can say that the actions of the trustees are not conducive to the best administration, that our property is not being well managed.
We can say that anyway.
But we cannot do anything about it.

Just as much as you ever
have.
Could parliament to-day, if it desired, refuse to vote the salaries of the directors or the management?
No, the directors are not paid by parliament.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The president was, under a contract made by order in council, but the money had to be provided by the railway.
I think the Prime Minister makes a mistake. The salary of the president was paid out of income.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is what I said.

The point is that these men are to be given extraordinary power. They are vested with ownership and control-practical ownership; the Prime Minister himself said they were to act as receivers in bankruptcy-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Not in bankruptcy.

These men must be controlled by someone, otherwise they can play ducks and drakes with the property of the people and no one in this house can prevent it. The government itself cannot. The people of Canada have no way of taking their own property out of the control of these three men. I think that is an abnormal state of affairs in a country that prides itself on being a democracy. Unless in some way we provide that they shall be obliged to come before parliament to have their salaries voted we shall be setting up in this country something which not only we but probably future generations will greatly regret, because these men through the method of appointment are practically self-perpetuating. During the course of the debate on the second reading the Prime Minister pointed out that it was quite possible that following a referendum an amalgamation of the two railroads might be brought about. But these directors, so long as there were assets in the Canadian National Railways to pay their salaries, would remain, and we could not do anything about it except by an address of both houses. No political party, no majority of the people of Canada could remove these trustees.

Does my hon. friend suggest that under section 12, if this House of Commons asked the trustees or some of them to come before a committee of this house, as I expect it will, to discuss the reasons why they needed this money, they could refuse?

C.N.R.-C.r.R. Bill

I am talking about their salaries now. The only way we could get rid of them would be to stop paying their salaries. That is the only way I can see to get rid of these men if they were not performing their duties properly, or if the people of this country decided that an act which we are now passing, though it may be proper to put into effect during a time of emergency, was not a proper measure for the administration of our national railways at another time. If the emergency disappears we may not need these trustees, but we cannot get rid of them. We have no control over them unless we vote their salaries.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I think the hon. gentleman might have started the rest of my observation, that this parliament has power to repeal this statute next session, and the trustees would then cease to hold office. A parliament that enacts can always repeal. If it were found that the trustees abused their power, did not properly discharge their duties, I have no doubt that no government would hestitate for a moment to take the necessary action to repeal the whole statute.
Suppose the Senate refuses?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I said parliament.

Does the Prime Minister
suggest that in order to get rid of the trustees we should repeal the whole act?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Repeal the section. It
is nothing new in parliamentary practice ; it has been done frequently and will continue to be done. Whether or not it gives ground for a claim for compensation is another matter. There is pending now before the privy council an appeal taken by a former member of the appeal courts from a judgment of the Supreme Court of Canada because as a result of legislation passed in 1930 an office was abolished and it was contended that there was a right to compensation. This parliament must be reasonable, this committee must be reasonable. We are facing what I think is very properly described as emergency in transportation matters. Parliament may desire to add to this bill ait another session, and I cannot contemplate the desirability of the committee wrangling over the salaries paid to the trustees. I believe that in the case of one of the great institutions of this country an effort was once made by a shareholder to ascertain what salary was paid to the president, and the directors declined to give the information. Only last week the government of the province of Ontario declined to make known the salaries paid to the hydro commissioners. The general prin-

ciple followed in British countries has been noit to discuss among the shareholders the compensation paid to the officers of the enterprise. But there always has to be included * in the reports to the Interstate Commerce Commission in the United States, and in this country to our Board of Railway Commissioners, I think, a statement of what the salaries are. The usual method taken by shareholders when they are dissatisfied with their officers is, at the annual meeting, to pass a vote of non-confidence in their directors; and that means that, although the directors retire by rotation, as they do in most companies nowadays in order to preserve continuity of policy, nevertheless, a motion of censure passed on directors has usually resulted in the disappearance of that board by resignation. I do not apprehend that there is any difficulty in a matter of this kind.
I do not think that we want to go over a bill of this character with a fine comb for the purpose of seeing that every possible contingency should be anticipated.
Why not?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The answer is obvious.
What we are trying to do is to lay down a principle and embody it in the form of a statute, and you can test any administrative statute of this kind only in the light of experience; so that if it is found defective at this or that point, parliament, which meets every year and is only for a few months not in session, can take proper measures to remedy such defects. I for one would not contend for a single moment that this is perfect legislation. It embodies the recommendation made by the commission-we will leave out altogether the question of the merits of that commission-and an effort has been made not to make it a contentious, narrow party measure but rather to ensure that there should be the freest opportunity for members of the committee to indicate where improvements might be effected-not, shall I say, to have narrow constructions placed on a broad measure of public control, but in the broadest possible sense to suggest where an improvement could be made here and an improvement there.
Dangers are foreseen with respect to amalgamation, and I for one am perfectly willing that the committee should take whatever steps it might think adequate to protect against that. Then there is the question of the abandonment of lines. Having lived in the west I know exactly how hon. members feel about that, the fear that there might be

C.NJi.-C.P.R. Bill
placed in the hands of some group the power to destroy branch line facilities. I think we have met that; what the minister said this afternoon completely meets that situation. And there are other suggestions of a like character. But when you get down to the question of arrangements between the employer and the employee, the trustees of the company, we have given large powers to the trustees, and this is the ground on which the commission took their position. They said: If you are to avoid the difficulties and pitfalls of political control and pressure, if you are to make this measure at all effective, you must hedge it round with such safeguards as will endeavour-we will put it that way at any rate-to secure public ownership of a great utility. When I hear the hon. member for North Waterloo talking about amalgamation of all lines under public ownership, with the history we have behind us, it seems to me that makes the whole thing a laughing stock, because the history we have behind the system is unfortunate in the sense that it has not worked well.

And what is the history of
privately-owned railroad companies all over the continent, including Canada?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The history of the private railway in this country is an amazing history. There is $120 of cash for every $100 of shares outstanding. It is the one company in all the world about which that can be said; and in point of efficient management-
Why doesn't it pay dividends?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
