It is not paying dividends; it is not paying dividends on preferred shares. But no one suggests that this is due to any other fact than the lessening of traffic. During the great period of expanding traffic for the railways, the Canadian National system, which came into being, after the late government assumed office, by the passing of an order in council after the judgment of the privy council in the Grand Trunk arbitration, and during the years following, in which there was a tremendous expansion involving the building of railways, branch lines and facilities, the commission finds that through it all runs the red thread of extravagance. Hon. gentlemen opposite dislike that, because they say that it is a criticism of themselves. Now, I do not think that the commission meant that, and I am not putting it in that light to the committee to-night. But everyone who is familiar with railways does admit that it is a fair 53719-2561
statement. We are so constituted in this young country, however, we take our politics so seriously at times and become so unwilling-
That cannot be blamed on the national railways alone. It can be applied to both railways.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Not the red thread of extravagance; that was applicable to one and not the other.
No, both.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: But the point is that one had an accumulated surplus of $100,000,000 or thereabouts and could afford to do things which the other could not, and you cannot compare incomparable things. For instance, the Pennsylvania system was able to do things which neither the old Wabash nor the Erie could do. And the Milwaukee, up to a certain point, was a most prosperous road and' could do things that the Northern Pacific and: other roads could not do.
But extravagance is always; extravagance.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes, but it is always' relative, having regard to resources and the ability to extend your earnings in proportion to your extravagances, if you call them extravagances. I think I can say that I am less a sinner with respect to these matters than any member of the committee, because I have a singularly consistent history with regard to the railway situation in this country. The hon. member for West Edmonton knows what my position has been. I have been as critical of the one as the other, and in 1908, standing in the Lyric theatre in Calgary, I made the statement that in my belief we were signing the death warrant of the successful conduct of transportation in Canada by endeavouring to build a third transcontinental in this country. I had no hesitancy in making that statement, and I have never changed my view. But now we are dealing with an emergency; we are grappling with a situation in which recrimina^-tions serve no purpose-
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
-and do not advance matters one bit. As to the suggestion that we should ask this parliament annually, with respect to these trustees, to discuss the question of their salaries, I am sure the hon. gentleman who proposes it knows that he cannot place a charge upon the country; it can be done only through the government. And the suggestion, it seems to me, is a negation of every principle that has hereto-

C.N.R.-C.FJt. Bill
fore governed in matters of this kind. The fact that it is the negative of everything that has been done does not prove that it is wrong, but you must show affirmatively that it has great merits to warrant its adoption, and there is no merit I can see that would warrant us in concluding that these trustees should have their salaries fixed by parliament annually. I do not think we could get the type of men we want for the position if we followed that course.

The Prime
Minister has been speaking with reference to the question of salaries, and I gather from his remarks that he has been defending the point of view of secrecy with respect to the remuneration to be paid officials of the railways. I am diametrically opposed to that view. The time has come when the more publicity there is with respect to public expenditures, and especially where they relate to a need for effecting economies, the better for all. The Prime Minister has used, particularly in relation to salaries, the expression, which is found in the commission's report, of the red thread of extravagance running through various expenditures. That red thread would not have been there had not the practice been followed of regarding as sacrosanct certain privileges surrounding those who hold great financial positions of one kind or another. If the present and the recent past has removed anything, it has removed this halo from the heads of great financiers. It has been made perfectly clear that there is no greater fiction in the world than the idea of the superman in business or finance, whether it be banking, railroading or any other form of industrial or commercial enterprise. I believe that this committee would be helping along a much needed reform if it insisted that instead of secrecy there be publicity with respect to all these matters of salary.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It has.

During the present debate the Minister of Railways made reference to certain salaries which he found were being paid to some of the officials of the Canadian National Railways. Personally I was astounded when I learned what some of those salaries were. Throughout the time I was Prime Minister I had no knowledge of what some of those salaries were, there were two reasons why I did not have that knowledge. The first was the avowed policy of the late administration, to allow the railway to be managed by the board of directors without any political interference. As far as I was

concerned, during the entire time I was in office I never sought directly or indirectly to influence the national railways with respect to any of these matters. The other reason was that, as mentioned, we also followed the practice of replying to many questions respecting salaries which were asked from time to time by stating that this information should not be given to parliament unless the railway itself was willing it Should be given. It was alleged that in making public this information an advantage would be given to its competitor. I think that practice was all nonsense. I believe the competitor as a rule knows exactly what is being paid. The practice amounts to a conspiracy between the competitors for their mutual advantage, as against the public interest or the interest of the particular concerns. I believe we should insist upon publicity in connection with all salaries. If it can be best had by having them reviewed in parliament, let it be done in that way. I am not referring merely to the salaries of the trustees, I am referring to the salaries and allowances paid to officials and others who have to do with the management and operation of the railways. If we could set an example in that regard we might be furthering a great reform which would be of immense service at the present time to this and other countries. I believe that such a reform will be insisted upon more and more in all countries. After all, there is very little about Which the average individual has not to give a public accounting. In connection with his personal income and matters of the kind he has to make a declaration which is sent into a government office. True enough it is protected, but the information is open to the Minister of Finance and the members of the government as well as to certain officials, if they wish to pry into affairs of this kind. There is hardly anything in which there is not full publicity with respect to the private means of individuals, why then should there not be publicity with respect to salaries which are paid out of the public treasury?
I think it is largely a false distinction to draw a line between those amounts which are paid out of the receipts of the railways and those paid out of the public treasury. What the latter amounts to, is determined by the former. The other day the committee was discussing the question of finding some means of compensating for the time they were out of employment, or until they could obtain other employment, the men who would be thrown out of employment as a result of economies effected. It was argued in the com-

C.N.R.-C.PJI. Bill
mittee, and ruled by the chairman that such a motion was out of order because if carried it would impose a burden upon the public treasury. The intent of the motion was that the money required should come out of or be a first charge upon the receipts of the railways themselves. After all, amounts which parliament will have to make good When meeting any deficit will always bear a relationship to the receipts of the railways, so in this discussion we should not try to draw too sharp a line between what is going to be a matter	of	expenditure	coming	under	theheading of what the railway itself provides from its revenues, and what is going to be a matter	of	expenditure	coming	under	the
heading of what this parliament will have to provide. It seems to me that the matter of the budget as a whole is one of national concern and ought so to be viewed.
May I say this further word? Either this parliament is supporting a policy of government ownership and control, or it is not. If the ministry feel that the time has come when we should not have government ownership and control, let them say so and bring in a measure to that effect. Let them abolish public ownership and control and turn the railways over to a private concern. If the ministry feel that they wish to retain government ownership but do not wish to have public control, let them bring in a measure to that effect, and say distinctly that they are through with the public control of railways. This important matter should not be camouflaged, and it seems to me that that is what is being done by this bill. The ministry is taking the railway property which is owned by the people of Canada, and turning it over to three private individuals to do with as they please. They are saying to these three individuals: You run this railroad as you please, independent altogether of the parliament of Canada and the approval of the governor in council. Where is there a scintilla of public control in that? It is government ownership with private control of the most exclusive type. It is giving a monopoly of control to three men, a monopoly of control and power which does not exist with respect to any other railway in this or any other country in the world. So far as the Canadian Pacific Railway is concerned, the operating forces are subject to the policies laid down by the directors who are considerable in number. We are discussing having only three directors while the Canadian Pacific have something like seventeen. May I here in passing point out something which I think should have been mentioned before? The provision for a large number of directors is one
which was put into the original statute by hon. members opposite. If there were too many directors appointed by the late government, it was 'because the late government took the act as they found it, and appointed directors to the number which was provided by the statute as passed by the previous administration.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: As a matter of fact, we increased it so as to give representation to all.

Yes, the number of directors was increased from fifteen to seventeen by the present government. What I am pointing out is this: In this particular measure the government is proposing to give complete control to three persons. If the railway were being handed over to another company, a purely private concern, to run, there would not be anything like the absolute private control which is provided for in this particular measure. Such a company would require that at least its shareholders should know What its directors were doing. Under this measure, this parliament, which represents the shareholders of the National railways, is parting absolutely with its control, unless in some way the budget and its details can be brought here to receive both discussion by and the approval of parliament.
I rose more particularly to speak in connection with the publicity which should be given to expenditures, particularly those made in the form of salaries, and I would like to conclude by reemphasizing this point. I believe that we in parliament would have escaped some of the criticism which has been made if we had had a provision in our original enactment to provide for giving to parliament the fullest information with regard to all expenditures made in the form of salaries. If this is an error which has been made in the past, let us not repeat it by following a practice which will make for even greater secrecy with respect to the expenditure of public money.

Mr. Chairman, I want to
assure the Prime Minister and the members of the committee that I have no desire to be unduly critical of the provisions of this bill. I would not be making any reference to the subject of the discussion this afternoon were it not for the fact that the Prime Minister referred to the matter of amalgamation. In answer to a question which he asked this afternoon, I said that I was in favour of amalgamation under public and not private ownership. Perhaps I should have said what was in my mind when I spoke on the second

C.NH.-C.P.R. Bill
reading of this bill, but I will do so now. I realize that amalgamation could not come at the present moment, but when it does come, it should come under public and not private ownership. Just in passing, I may say that I have no desire to deal at any length with this particular phase of the matter, but in my opinion amalgamation will have to come. This government will have to face that problem just as it will have to face some other things which so far it has not had either the inclination or the courage to face.
Something was said about the reference by the royal commission to the red thread of extravagance which had run through the Canadian National Railways. I do not want to make any invidious comparison but I think it is known to everyone that the same description could be applied to the operations of another railway. If the red thread of extravagance did in fact run through the operations of the Canadian National Railways to any extent, it also ran through the operations of the other railroad.
Now with regard to the clause under discussion and the suggestion made by the hon. member for Quebec South, I would say that I am in favour of that only in case the government refuse to accept what seems to me the reasonable alternative. The suggestion advanced by the hon. member for Quebec South is that by having the salaries voted by parliament we would have some measure of control over the board of trustees. I think we should have some measure of control over that board. I do not particularly favour this method, by having parliament vote the salaries, and just here let me say that I am one of those who would like as little interference as possible with these trustees when they take over the management of this railway. But I want to point out that if the bill goes through as it stands now the House of Commons or the government itself, and I am speaking now of the cabinet, has no power whatever to get rid of that board if it should desire to do so. The members of the board will be appointed for terms of seven years, and there is no means provided for dispensing with their services except by the vote of both houses of parliament. If we have any belief whatever in democratic government I think the control of the board should rest not with 'both houses of parliament but with the House of Commons or the executive itself. That is the point I desire to make.
It was Stated during the debate on the second reading, I think by the Prime Minister, that the board of trustees could not spend a sou without the consent of the governor in

council. I think the Prime Minister was wrong in that statement; perhaps he did not mean exactly what he said, because this parliament and this government have absolutely nothing to do with the expenditure of the operating revenues of the railway. They are perfectly free to do as they please with revenues amounting to $150,000,000 or $160,000,000, and that was the case under the old dispensation.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I think the hon. gentleman has not correctly quoted me, I wras dealing with capital expenditures.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Just one word in reply, Mr. Chairman. It is not often that the right hon. leader of the opposition and myself are in accord. If the right hon. gentleman gathered from what I said that I believed in secrecy with regard to everything connected with public companies he was entirely in error. I have expressed myself very freely during the last two years or so with respect to that matter. There have been wrecks of companies in this country which, if this parliament had possessed jurisdiction, certainly would have been heard of; I say that to the right hon. gentleman now. It is true they happened under circumstances which precluded the possibility of this parliament exercising control, but I am wholly in sympathy with the effort that has been made during the past few weeks by those interested in one corporation to obtain information as to how the money they paid into that corporation was invested. Certainly I am of the opinion that publicity is the surest cure for many of the corporate evils that have grown up in the world in the last few years. About that there is no doubt;
I am wholly in accord with that view. I have expressed myself perhaps too freely in that regard, in the view of some of my old time personal friends. But I put this to the committee, and I put it very fairly: it is an altogether different thing to throw into this house the discussion from year to year of the salary you are going to pay a trustee. Knowledge must be given, of course, but to say that this parliament is to vote that sum implies that the Minister of Finance will introduce it as an estimate, and if he introduces the salaries of the trustees as an estimate why should not that practice be followed in regard to the rest of the officials of the railway as well? That would negative the very object this bill has in view. Section 12 provides that the annual budget of the national railways shall be under the control of the trustees.

Does not the Prime Minister think the wording of this clause is obscure? The very fact that you mention the annual budget suggests that such a budget should be presented to parliament. In the discussion on the resolution I think that was why the Prime Minister left us under the impression that the annual budget of the Canadian National would be submitted to the house.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: the courts, so I shall do no more than merely direct attention to it. This parliament has the right to repeal any of these sections ait any time if it so desires.
But not the House of Commons.
The House of Commons has not the power.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The House of Commons, no. It is rather difficult to understand any hon. member of this house, and I think the leader of the opposition will agree with me, suggesting that there are not two houses of parliament.
I am not suggesting that.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The suggestion is that
one constitutes parliament; it does not. There are three estates of the realm.
We all know that.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The Commons, the Senate and the crown. The hon. gentleman may know it, but he certainly did not say it. What he said was that the House of Commons should determine these things.

That is exactly what I
meant.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
That it wias the only
body that should deal with these matters. Now parliament is the body that deals with them, and parliament consists of two chambers, not one, and I do submit when it is suggested that one body should usurp all the functions of parliament, that that is a mistake. Why is it that the tenure of office of judges has been surrounded with the conditions which have been applied thereto?
They administer the law; they do not make it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: But I say that this is an endeavour to put the administrative trustees in a position where they at least could feel that they could exercise independent judgment without having to respond to political convictions.
They are doing much more than administering.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
No, they are only administering in the large sense, because administration involves all the functions mentioned in the bill. They are essentially the directing administrators as trustees of this property.

The hon. member for North Bruce (Mr. Malcolm) said that the chairman should be a railroad man. The statute provides that the operating official of the road as distinguished from the executive head of the road shall be the operating man. The executive head of the road, the chairman of the board of trustees, the man who discharges with relation to this undertaking what is discharged by the executive committee, for instance, of the great transcontinental railroads of the United States, which have their head offices in Omaha or Kansas City, but their executive committees in New York-they have their executive offices in the city of New York, why? Because the financial concern of a railroad enterprise is of such paramount importance. This statute contemplates that the operating official-the name used is president, which might lead to some conflict of view; I do not know that it is the best word that could be used; some other word might be more apt

is the man who is responsible for operations. But so far as the board of trustees is concerned, its functions must necessarily be largely concerned with what you might call the financial picture as distinguished from the other side of it. When you hear talk about the humanities of the situation, the fact is that the humanities of the situation are dealt with by the operating head of the road and by the men themselves. Everyone who knows the history of railroads is aware of the fact that in their unions the men have established safeguards to protect themselves in the most ample manner, and the relations between them and the road itself are usually dealt with at conferences between the men and the president and the officials of the operating section of the road. You see in the paper, for instance, that the heads of the union organizations have met such and such operating officials, and if they are unable to agree, they have a board. So this is an effort at least to meet an emergency situation in which the Canadian people are called upon to pay something over one million dollars a week.
Quite so, an emergency situation.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Quite so, and in this emergency the board is to be appointed-
But the legislation provides for permanent appointments, for the trustees acting continuously.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It certainly does.

The emergency is not
going to be everlasting.

C.N.R.-C.P.R. Bill

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
No, but you co-uld not
in a bill give any form or shape to a policy if you limited its application to a particular period of time. I think the hon. member is too familiar with business not to say that is so; particularly when dealing with a large public utility, that one of the dangers in endeavouring to limit the time in which a policy is to be operative is that by so doing you defeat your own end. But the main concern of this board of trustees, I would once more urge upon the committee, which the commission had in mind was to endeavour to secure such administration of this property as would relieve the taxpayers of Canada from paying one million dollars a week.
The other side of it, the humanity side of it which has been mentioned, is left largely to be dealt with by the president and the various officials of the road in conferences with the unions, such as have always taken place and at which adequate measures have been taken for safeguarding the interests of all who might be concerned.
But the great concern of this legislation is to endeavour to provide a body of men of such competence as will ensure that these continuing deficits will vanish. That is the story as I appreciate it and as it has been put to me, and as I understand the whole purpose for which the commission was created and the action taken.
Coming back to the amendment, I submit that it is not the proper form of an amendment to be moved in this house because it asks to put a charge on the revenues of the dominion. The leader of the opposition says that you cannot sharply divide where deficits begin and surpluses end, but we all know the difference between operating revenues and operating expenses, and included in the operating expenses are the salaries of the transportation officials, not. only transportation in the narrow sense but of all those who constitute the personnel operating the railway. It would be an anomalous situation if we appointed a board of trustees and provided that they shall be paid by parliament although operating a system whose revenues under the law they control. I think it is not only out of order to suggest that an amendment be moved by a private member which charges the Finance minister with introducing in parliament an estimate, which is altogether improper as I understand the constitutional workings of our law, but it goes further and would precipitate into this house a discussion from time to time as to whether or not we shall vote to these men every year a sum of money for salaries. Their salaries will undoubtedly be known to everybody. The government under the statute must take the responsibility for fixing those salaries. If they are too high the house will censure the government; if they are not adequate we shall not be able to get the trustees.

When I spoke on the
second reading of this bill I said that my principal objection to the legislation was that the Prime Minister had distinctly pointed out what he always points out when he arises, that we are dealing with an emergency, and yet the bill which is to deal with an emergency appoints trustees who cannot be dismissed. If the Prime Minister or the Minister of Railways would incorporate in this legislation a fixed period of time, say five years, within which these men were to be given absolute power, I would support that phase of the legislation very freely, but I do point out to the Prime Minister and to the minister that in this legislation we are just continuing the system we had before under the old act, the system which was criticized in the last parliament, the system by which the directors can spend every dollar of operating revenue which they receive and spend it as extravagantly as they see fit. No one is of the opinion that railway tonnage will remain at its present low level. Everyone believes that general business conditions will improve. When they do improve, and the operating revenues of the railways are sufficiently great, not only should interest be paid to the bondholders, as it was in one or two successful years under the leadership of the late Sir Henry Thornton, but there should be provision for substantial payments towards those moneys which the parliament of Canada has advanced. I contend under this legislation we are appointing these men permanently, and giving them exactly the same power as Sir Henry Thornton had. I contend that this is an emergent situation. Probably if it were private business it would be in liquidation, and if it were in liquidation it would be in the same position as some American roads in connection with which receivers have been appointed. Yet, being guaranteed by the people of Canada, these bonds have to be met; the road being the property of the Canadian people it cannot go into liquidation. Therefore the only alternative is to appoint, one, two, three, four or five men, whatever number the government decides upon, to act as trustees. I object strongly to these trustees being appointed for a continuous period of time. They are not like judges; there can be no comparison between them and judges. A
C.N.R.-C.P.R. Bill

judge is appointed to administer the laws which this parliament makes, and all parliament has to do is to change that law. These men are appointed to administer a great national utility, and to administer it with such a free hand that every dollar of revenue they receive may be spent in operating expenses. This parliament or government has no control over them, unless both houses of parliament agree, which is not very likely. I have no doubt the hon. member for Quebec South would withdraw his amendment if these men were appointed for a definite period of years- say five years.

I admit I am surprised at
the attitude taken by the Prime Minister in connection with observations which have been, made from this side of the house. He complains that we have been unduly critical. He urges us to bless this bill, whether it be good or bad. He will recollect, at any rate I know the Minister of Railways will, that when the bill was introduced he besought our cooperation.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: And I did it again tonight.

We are endeavouring to
give co-operation. On the last occasion when the bill was presented we suggested certain amendments which were discussed and which were accepted to-day. To-day we are pointing out-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Two of them were promised before the house ever went into com-nnittee. It has taken six hours to talk about them.

I am now discussing an
amendment which provides that the Board of Railway Commissioners shall have some control over the 'tearing up of branch lines. To the best of my knowledge-and I followed the debate on this bill very closely-there was no such promise made.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It was stated section 23 applied; that must relieve any doubt.

It was argued at great
length by the Prime Minister that section 23 did apply. Evidently he is not quite sure of it. We will now find some of the theories laid down by the Prime Minister with respect to ithe board of trustees of which he is not quite sure, either. A great many of us are not quite sure that we agree with him on the position he takes. He has said the proposal we were making was something new. Since when is it new for the parliament of Canada to have oontrol over moneys ex-

pended and derived from the taxpayers? Since when is it new for the House of Commons to know what salaries are being paid for the administration of its property?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
No one has said there
is any objection to knowing what they are.

Surely the Prime Minister
is not serious when he tells us we ought to be satisfied to know what they are. After all our duty as members is to see that the moneys raised from the taxpayers are spent in the interests of those taxpayers, and our further duty is to oontrol the expenditure of that money. If there is anything new in the present situation, then it is a new position which is now being created. These men mentioned in the bill are called trustees; we are told they are not directors. As the right hon. gentleman pointed out, directors are elected annually. If shareholders are not satisfied with the directors they do not reeleot them. As a general rule trustees are under the control of a court. In 'the present instance, however, we have an example of a new species of administrator. We are setting up a railway dictator, or possibly three railway dictators. We are giving them seven yeans in which to operate, and providing that of their own volition their offices may be self-perpetuating. We are giving them practically perpetual control over property belonging to the people of Canada. The Prime Minister 'has said we may repeal the act. I know, and we all know, that the very moment any proposal is made to repeal the act or to repeal that section of it, we will be told that the national honour is at stake. Section 7 of the bill states:
No trustee shall be removed from office, nor suffer any reduction in salary, during the term for which he is appointed, unless for assigned cause and on address of the Senate and House of Commons of Canada.
I suggest this is a contract which the parliament of Canada enters into with trustees, and by that contract we cannot remove them. Let us suppose that two of the trustees wish to reduce their salaries, but that the third man declines, and states, "There can be no reduction of my salary." We could not do it, and the other trustees could not do it. A change could be made only for assigned cause and on address of the Senate and House of Commons of Canada. I submit the proposal which we are making, namely that the salaries should in some way be within the control of the House of Commons of Canada, is reasonable and logical, and is not new. There is nothing revolutionary about it, and the suggestion represents one of the fundamental rights of parliament.

The Prime Minister states he wishes to place these men above all suspicion of political interference. In that connection I wish to repeat what I said on another occasion, namely that the Duff commission did not find that under the former regime, or the present one, officials were interfered with either by ministers or by members of parliament in connection with the detailed operations of the road. I assume that if the new trustees to be appointed are men of as high calibre as those who were made directors, those trustees will not be interfered with, either. But the serious political interference comes in when branch lines are unloaded, and that interference can be carried on when the trustees are appointed and when-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: There are not any branch lines left; they have all been taken up.
When the matter was under discussion before I pointed out that there was the Temiscouata railroad, and the Pacific Great Eastern, which is worth about $50,000,000.
Without the sanction and guarantee of parliament they could not take over a railway.
That is the point I am trying to make. Parliament could foist on these trustees any branch line railway now independently existing in Canada.
Not if the trustees did not wish to take it.

There is nothing to prevent the introduction of a bill providing for the payment for the Pacific Great Eastern or the Temiscouata railway of so many million dollars, and saying that this railway shall belong to the Canadian National system.
Do you believe in parliamentary government?

I do, but the argument of the minister was that we are appointing these men for seven years, making them dictators so that they will get away from political interference. What I am endeavouring to make clear is that the political interference which may have bedevilled this road in the minds of some hon. gentlemen opposite and of a section of the public is political interference which put branch lines over on the Canadian National; not that which might interefere with detailed operation, such as the appointment of a watchman. These trustees are not getting us away from political interference in the harmful sense; that is the point I am trying to make. If they are not going to do
any good to the road other than keep some member of parliament from a back concession from having one of his friends appointed brakeman or having someone appointed to sweep out the Union station here, if that is all we are going to appoint dictators for, I submit that one year is enough, or perhaps six months. That is the position I take.

Mr. Chairman,
I do not know whether the committee are aware that this provision, namely that the trustees shall not be removed except by an address by both houses of parliament, is something which was not in-any way recommended by the Duff commission. It is a provision put in by the present ministry, or at their instigation. The Duff commission does not make any suggestion of the kind. The self-perpetuating feature of the trusteeship comes from the Drayton-Acworth commission report, and in that connection the remarks of one of those commissioners are very significant. Mr. Smith, one of the commissioners, used these words as part of his report to parliament-*
He was a minority.

Yes, but it is interesting to see what he said:
I am unable to join my colleagues in their recommendations. They propose that practically all of the railways in Canada, except the Canadian Pacific and the American lines, shall be turned over to a corporation to be managed by a board of trustees appointed by government. They insist that this board is to be permanent and self-perpetuating. I do not know by what means one parliament can bind its successors to a given policy, especially in so simple a matter as changing the organization of a government board. My friends seek to avoid government ownership and operation, in fact condemn it as inadvisable, but propose a plan which contains so many elements of danger in the direction which is sought to be avoided that I am unable to join them.
I direct the attention of the committee to what is there said about the desire to avoid government ownership and operation. Mr. Smith's friends on the commission, the majority, according to the other commissioner, wished to avoid government ownership and operation, and to make it impossible, and according to Mr. Smith one of the means taken to make it impossible was to make the trustee board self-perpetuating. I submit that as long as we have government control or purport to have it and are going to endeavour to carry it out, we should not enact legislation which is definitely designed to make government control impossible.
Progress reported.
